articles.title: Internal DOJ documents tell story on caseload surge amid Trump immigration moves
articles.summary: A push to force all migrants to await deportation from detention and other Trump administration immigration policies have pushed the number of cases to record highs for the Department of Justice (DOJ) branch that handles such litigation. The Hill recently obtained internal DOJ metrics showing staff levels have plummeted while the department is also handling…
articles.body:
A push to force all migrants to await deportation from detention and other Trump administration immigration policies have pushed the number of cases to record highs for the Department of Justice (DOJ) branch that handles such litigation.

The Hill recently obtained internal DOJ metrics showing staff levels have plummeted while the department is also handling unprecedented caseloads.

But that dynamic was particularly pronounced in the civil division’s Office of Immigration Litigation (OIL), which has lost nearly 80 attorneys as workload has jumped 63 percent.

There are multiple factors at play behind the surge.

“I think there are two big drivers,” said Margy O’Herron, a former official in the deputy attorney general’s office during the Biden administration who oversaw immigration work.

“OIL represents the government in cases where the Board [of Immigration Appeals] denies asylum,” she said, noting that grants of the protection are at a “historic low.”

The other is the Trump administration’s decision to cut off bond hearings for migrants, prompting a wave of habeas petitions from migrants demanding the government justify why they are being held.

“The habeas cases have grown significantly, because the administration has begun detaining people who have no criminal history, have been in the country for a long time, and would not have been detained under prior administrations. Now they’re holding them in immigration jails,” said O’Herron, now a senior fellow at the Brennan Center.

There may also be another wave of new cases coming that would not be reflected in the data obtained by The Hill: the Trump administration’s effort to boost denaturalizations .

The DOJ boasted Monday that it had filed 40 denaturalization cases, calling it “the largest volume of complaints submitted in a single period under the Trump administration,” from late August to early October.

One former OIL attorney said staffers there have been given a goal to file 300 such cases.

The DOJ did not respond to request for comment for this story.

OIL’s staff fell from 320 attorneys at the start of the Trump administration down to 243 in August. Meanwhile, cases handled by the branch have climbed from roughly 7,700 to nearly 9,500.

It’s not just OIL; the DOJ has been bleeding staff across its civil division as waves of attorneys have left the department.

But the Trump administration’s interest in immigration has piled on the workload for the diminished crop of attorneys in that branch.

The administration has also remade the immigration courts managed under the DOJ, including the Board of Immigration Appeals — firing and replacing many immigration judges in the system.

Asylum grants have been declining for years, but they’ve plunged to new lows under President Trump. While grant rates dropped from about 50 percent to the low 30s under the Biden administration, just 5.5 percent of asylum applicants as of June received grants, according to data from the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse (TRAC).

Those who appeal their denials have their cases heard in the federal appeals court system, which is handled by OIL.

“Because there’s so many denials, and there will be more, more cases are going to be appealed into federal court,” O’Herron said.

But perhaps the biggest shift in casework has been due to the overwhelming number of migrants filing habeas petitions in an effort to leave detention while they fight their removal case in immigration court.

Gregory Chen, senior director of government relations at the American Immigration Lawyers Association, said the denial of bond hearings is “the most obvious reason for the surge.”

Immigration courts for years had released migrants on bond as their cases were pending, but the Trump administration brought an end to such hearings — a policy set to be reviewed by the Supreme Court later this term.

“Judges use a standard two-prong analysis, which is whether the person is a flight risk or poses a public safety threat,” Chen said, noting the costly alternative of detaining people, with nearly 70,000 migrants currently held in detention.

“It’s just not humane or fair to be forcing people to go through multiple layers of expensive, costly litigation to try to get the opportunity to come before a judge and tell the judge that they shouldn’t be denied their freedom,” he continued. “American taxpayers should really be angry that the Trump administration has created essentially a multiple-tiered structure, giving people the runaround if they want to ask a judge to consider where they need to be detained, and that’s a tremendous waste of taxpayer dollars.”

In the early days of the Trump administration — March 2025 — just 105 people had filed habeas petitions to seek their release.

But such cases have soared this year. Data from TRAC shows that in February and March 2026, the most recent data, more than 8,000 and 9,000 habeas cases were filed monthly.

For the most part, migrants have been successful in court.

A June analysis from Politico found that judges had sided with migrants on habeas cases more than 15,000 times but sided with the administration in just 2,200 cases.

The same dynamic has played out as the policy has made its way through appeals courts.

“Nine of 11 circuits have also ruled against the government, so it’s not a strong case for the government to bring. But I think they’re going to take their chances with the Supreme Court and hope that their interpretation gets upheld. If it does, it would really remake the way that immigration detention works in this country,” O’Herron said.

“It would take huge numbers of people with no conviction, with strong ties to the United States, including citizen family members, citizen children, American employers, and put them in jail while they wait to challenge their cases.”

Chen noted detention has been a tool for the Trump administration to pressure migrants to give up their case and agree to be deported.

“This administration has effectively weaponized immigration detention as a way to intimidate and frighten people away from getting their fair day in court on their case,” he said.

“Detaining people while they’re waiting for the case to be decided is a horrendously frightening thing for anybody because the conditions are harsh and often inhumane, and people suffer poor conditions as well as abuses in detention, and many people simply give up, even if they have a strong case for their legal relief to be able to stay in the United States, just because they’re too afraid to stay another day, another night in a detention cell.”

articles.title: Will Rubio, Ossoff and Ocasio-Cortez run for president?
articles.summary: Politicians eyeing a White House run typically utter the words “I’m not interested” in running for president. Much of the time, the politicians inevitably jump into the race. And sometimes — as was the case with Barack Obama when he famously declared in 2006 that he “will not” run for president — they win. But…
articles.body:
Politicians eyeing a White House run typically utter the words “I’m not interested” in running for president.

Much of the time, the politicians inevitably jump into the race. And sometimes — as was the case with Barack Obama when he famously declared in 2006 that he “will not” run for president — they win.

But as the field of would-be 2028 candidates comes into view, some of the politicians whose names have been bandied about are privately telling allies, aides, donors and others in their circles that they’re lukewarm on actually running.

Sen. Jon Ossoff, who has risen on the wish lists of a number of Democrats in recent months as he runs for reelection in Georgia, has said publicly that he has no interest in a White House bid.

“I have zero interest in running for president in 2028,” the senator told WSB-TV in Atlanta last month.

Privately, Ossoff has expressed the same sentiment to allies, even those who are pushing him into the presidential ring by telling the senator that this is his moment to run for the White House.

“I think that’s real,” said one Democratic strategist who has spoken to those in Ossoff’s inner circle. “I don’t think the interest is there, at least for this upcoming cycle.”

One donor added that in a crowded field with more than a dozen candidates and with the Democratic primary map changing for the next cycle “it seems a little tougher for someone like him and maybe he realizes that.”

The donor explained that while South Carolina could be a good state for Ossoff because he’s proven he can win in the South, the next few states — including Nevada and New Mexico — could be a tougher climb.

Another prospective candidate, Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, who has also risen in the ranks of popular Democrats who could one day run for higher office, has told some in her orbit that she may sit out the upcoming election and take some time off.

She echoed those comments in an interview with Fox2 in Detroit, saying, “I think there will be a robust group of people running for president. I will not be one of them in 2028, I can tell you that.”

Whitmer also told a crowd at an annual policy conference in her state that she wanted to take “a little bit of a break” and has spoken to other politicians on both sides of the aisle about doing so.

But she has also sought to remain part of the public discussion on a potential 2028 run, telling a panel in May “never say never.”

“I never thought I would run for governor, so I guess I should know better,” Whitmer said.

More recently, she played coy during a sit-down with California Gov. Gavin Newsom — who has been anything but shy about his interests in running for president.

“I have a bug in that I want to stay involved,” she told Newsom on his podcast, after he inferred that she still has “a bug” and somewhat mockingly urged her to “tell the truth.

“The bug isn’t ‘I got to run for office,’” she said.

Democratic strategist Eddie Vale explained that while there’s a good deal of attention paid to the reasons candidates decide to run for office, “there are a lot of reasons not to.”

“No matter what job you have had, or what campaign you have run before, nothing is comparable to a presidential run,” Vale said. “From the time on the road to scrutiny of every word you have ever said, to the pressure on your family, it kind of makes ‘Odyssey’ look like a stroll around the Mediterranean.”

“For a lot of people it is a very logical answer that putting yourself and your family through it is not worth the small chance of being the one who actually wins,” he said.

On the Republican side, there has been chatter for months about whether Secretary of State Marco Rubio will enter the GOP primary in 2028.

Rubio has told donors and other allies that he will not run, particularly against Vice President Vance, sources say.

Some Republicans — including those in his orbit — interpret that to mean that he wants to take a break from politics, possibly write a book, and put some space between himself and President Trump, who is facing low approval ratings and dissatisfaction from voters about issues including the economy.

“I think he’s smart and knows that a little bit of distance could go a long way,” one Republican strategist said.

But one year in politics is a long time, and politicians realize they may not get another chance. Rubio is also seen by many Republicans as a GOP candidate who could win in 2028 in a general election.

In a New York Times interview last month, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), who is considering a run for the Senate and also a campaign for president, was open about her calculus on running and how she may only get one shot at a presidential run, particularly at a moment when progressives and democratic socialists are gaining steam in her party.

“There’s an argument that some make that this is a very unique political window and, oftentimes in politics, you do only get one shot,” she said in the interview.

Obama decided that he would run nine months after he told the late Tim Russert on NBC’s “Meet the Press” that he would not run.

When Russert confronted him on his earlier insistence that he would not run, Obama explained, “That was how I was thinking at the time.” But he said that the enthusiasm around the country had forced him to reexamine his political aspirations.

Democratic strategist Joel Payne, who has worked on a few presidential campaigns including Hillary Clinton’s 2016 run, said candidates have to “seize the moment” when it’s the right time.

“Political history is full of individuals who did not strike while the iron is hot,” Payne said. “I think when the moment calls, you gotta be ready to pick up the phone.”

articles.title: The Senate races most likely to flip less than a month from Election Day
articles.summary: The race for control of the Senate is heating up, with forecasters increasingly moving races in the Democrats’ direction less than a month out from the election. Last week, nonpartisan election forecasters Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball at the University of Virginia Center for Politics shifted Senate races in Kansas, New Hampshire,…
articles.body:
The race for control of the Senate is heating up, with forecasters increasingly moving races in the Democrats’ direction less than a month out from the election.

Last week, nonpartisan election forecasters Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball at the University of Virginia Center for Politics shifted Senate races in Kansas, New Hampshire, North Carolina, Alaska and South Carolina in Democrats’ favor.

President Trump’s tanking approval ratings and high costs associated with the war in Iran and the tariff war with Canada are making it difficult for Republicans to navigate the persistent headwinds, though some candidates have broken with the president on certain issues as they seek to differentiate themselves from the White House and national party.

And while Democrats see a favorable political environment, it’s not guaranteed that it will be enough to push them into majority-making territory.

Here’s a look at the Senate races most likely to flip less than one month before Election Day.

The Tar Heel State has often served as Democrats’ metaphorical “Lucy and the football,” disappointing the party time and again at the presidential and Senate level, though they’ve fared better in gubernatorial races.

But the party notched a strong recruit in former Gov. Roy Cooper, with recent polling showing him leading former Republican National Committee Chair Michael Whatley by anywhere from single to double digits.

The Senate Leadership Fund, the super PAC aligned with Senate GOP leadership, has pulled money from the race, and the Senate Majority PAC, the super PAC aligned with Senate Democratic leadership, has as well, though to a lesser extent. However, that doesn’t mean either group has withdrawn entirely from the race financially.

Alaska has also served as an unexpected bright spot for Democrats thanks to another strong recruit in former Rep. Mary Peltola.

The state is generally reliably Republican, with Trump winning the state by 13 points in 2024. However, Sabato’s Crystal Ball moved the state into the “lean Democrat” category — Cook Political Report rates it as a “toss-up” — given several recent surveys from strong pollsters.

Another notable sign is the fact that Vice President Vance has campaigned in the state, while the president is expected to be there this week. Still, J. Miles Coleman and Kyle Kondik of Sabato’s Crystal Ball wrote on Tuesday in an analysis that Sullivan is a tough incumbent to beat.

“Though Alaska is, demographically, one of the youngest states, both the AARP poll and the more recent NYT poll show Sullivan carrying voters older than 45,” they wrote. “A couple of other pollsters have also shown a closer race: a late September poll from Quantus Insights had the race tied, while a couple of other conservative pollsters had Sullivan narrowly leading.”

Peltola also came under scrutiny after The New York Times reported last month about the former congresswoman’s allegedly abusive behavior toward staff — accusations her campaign has denied while noting that she has “sometimes struggled to deal with her grief” from losing her husband and mother. It’s unclear from polling if that’s hurt her Senate bid against Sullivan.

Like many of the competitive Senate races being closely watched over the next month, the Ohio Senate race is regularly polling within the margin of error. Sen. Jon Husted (R) is running in a special election to complete the remainder of Vance’s term in the Senate against former Sen. Sherrod Brown, one of the rare Democrats who has won statewide in the Buckeye State.

Ohio has trended away from Democrats in recent cycles, so much so that it wasn’t even considered one of the six swing states during the 2024 presidential election. And Brown’s loss to Sen. Bernie Moreno (R) that same cycle was another indicator of Ohio’s rightward shift.

As some news outlets like the Times have noted , some voters still think Brown is the sitting senator while Husted is lesser known to voters. If Ohio swings back toward Democrats next month, it would offer one of the first real signs that Democrats could be in for a very good night — and that they may be able to reverse some of their losses moving into the next election cycle.

Democrats have long tried to oust Sen. Susan Collins in past elections, but the GOP senator has proven to be a formidable candidate and is the only Senate Republican to represent a state former Vice President Kamala Harris won in 2024.

Former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson (D) replaced populist Graham Platner as Democrats’ nominee to take on Collins in the Pine Tree State after numerous scandals forced Platner out of the race.

Jackson and Democrats broadly have sought to hit Collins specifically for her vote to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who was among the majority in ruling to overturn Roe v. Wade in 2022. The issue is nuanced for the GOP senator, who supports access to abortion and has supported legislation aimed at codifying federal abortion access.

Democrats have also hit Collins over a recent ProPublica investigation that alleged the GOP senator was involved in a pay-to-play scheme aimed at garnering contributions in exchange for government contracts to the defense contractor Navatek. Collins and her campaign have vehemently denied the allegations , calling it a “partisan hit” and “offensive” and pointing out that the allegations came from a convicted felon.

It’s unclear how much the controversy will electorally impact Collins as polling in the race shows a tight contest, and the GOP senator has proven she can win in tough races.

Michigan is seen as one of Republicans’ best pickup opportunities this cycle with Sen. Gary Peters (D) retiring. Former Rep. Mike Rogers (R) narrowly lost to Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D) in 2024, making him a formidable recruit in the 2026 cycle.

Republicans were eager to have former Wayne County health director Abdul El-Sayed as their Democratic opponent instead of the more centrist Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.), seeing him as too far left for the swing state.

Yet, Rogers has increasingly taken positions that break with the Trump administration, such as calling for the war in Iran to end and calling for the tariff war with Canada to be resolved. He’s not the only Senate Republican candidate to do that this cycle, though the fact that he’s called on Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to make a deal with Canada underscores the urgency many GOP challengers are feeling to turn things around before next month.

The Lone Star State has been another figurative “Lucy and the football” for Democrats after former Rep. Beto O’Rourke (D) narrowly lost to Sen. Ted Cruz (R) in 2018. O’Rourke later lost by a wider margin against Gov. Greg Abbott (R) in the 2022 governor’s race.

Trump’s travel to Texas — where he made quips calling Republican Ken Paxton a “little controversial” and a “pain in the a–” — coupled with different leaked audio clips of Paxton trickling out last week have shown an increasingly volatile race. The president has even encouraged Paxton to debate Democrat James Talarico.

At the same time, Republicans have a clear edge in spending in Texas, which is an expensive state given its multiple media markets. The ad-tracking firm AdImpact reported on Friday that Republicans had spent more than $51 million alone in future ad buys in the state, while Democrats had committed nearly $5 million.

If Democrats flip the Iowa Senate seat in November, it will likely indicate a wave election. Handicapper Inside Elections rates the race as “tilt Republican,” though Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball have moved it slightly toward the Democrats and have called it a “toss-up” in recent months.

Republicans have a strong recruit in Rep. Ashley Hinson, and the Hawkeye State hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate since former Sen. Tom Harkin’s reelection in 2008. The state went for Trump by 13 points in 2024. Recent polling also has Hinson narrowly leading.

But forecasters have noted that the prices of fertilizer and gas are concerns in the state, and Hinson has gone as far as to call for Trump to end the war in Iran. AdImpact also noted that Iowa Democrats narrowly hold an edge there in future ad reservations — only one of eight competitive Senate races where that’s the case.

The Sunflower State’s Senate race turned into an unexpected marquee contest this cycle, with Democrat Adam Hamilton notching several high-profile endorsements , including from two former Republican governors. Kansas hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932, meaning Hamilton faces steep odds in attempting to topple Sen. Roger Marshall (R).

Marshall has received scrutiny more recently over his handling of taxpayer funds and for suing hundreds of patients over medical debt, while Hamilton has received scrutiny over his handling of a child sexual abuse scandal at his church.

An attorney for Marshall told MS NOW and the Kansas Reflector that the official office and campaign site both comply with campaign finance rules and Senate ethics rules. Marshall has also defended his decision to sue medical patients, saying he acted appropriately .

Hamilton told the Kansas Reflector he would have handled the initial reports of abuse, which were ultimately reported to officials, differently but also said that “there was no attempt at a cover-up” during the church’s investigation.

“Kansas has not elected a Democratic senator since 1932, and we’d still be surprised if that streak ends this year,” Kondik of Sabato’s Crystal Ball wrote last month , while noting the outlet was shifting the race slightly toward Democrats.

The Granite State will serve as Republicans’ second-best pickup opportunity should they have a better-than-expected Election Day. The GOP notched a strong recruit in former Sen. John Sununu, whose last name is a political dynasty in the state, and he’ll be running on the same ballot as Gov. Kelly Ayotte (R), who’s expected to win reelection next month.

But Cook Political Report’s Jessica Taylor suggested Trump’s underwater approval ratings in the state, current polling on the race and an expectation that Sununu could underperform Ayotte given how voters weigh federal and statewide races make Rep. Chris Pappas (D-N.H.) the favorite right now.

“This race could still end up being closer than it should be given the national environment,” Taylor wrote . “Democratic ads hitting Sununu for his own work for a lobbying firm seem to have penetrated, but Pappas — who weathered a barrage of attack ads over the summer for his now-husband’s lobbying work for Amazon — also has work to do in the closing weeks to rally voters who aren’t fans of the Democratic Party either.”

Four other races to watch: Minnesota, South Carolina, Nebraska and Georgia

The Senate races in Minnesota, South Carolina, Nebraska and Georgia are also being closely watched by both parties as the races take the temperature of electorates in more Democratic- and Republican-leaning states.

None of these states are expected to flip in November given their more partisan leanings, though upsets in any of these races would offer a telltale sign of a good night for one of the parties or another sleeper race observers missed.

articles.title: GOP looks for midterm enthusiasm boost from pro sports stars
articles.summary: Staring down a midterm Election Day that is looking increasingly bleak for Republicans, GOP candidates and President Trump are turning to major names in sports for a jolt of energy and publicity. Several current and former pro athletes in recent weeks have stumped for Republicans on the campaign trail or introduced GOP hopefuls to crowds…
articles.body:
Staring down a midterm Election Day that is looking increasingly bleak for Republicans, GOP candidates and President Trump are turning to major names in sports for a jolt of energy and publicity.

Several current and former pro athletes in recent weeks have stumped for Republicans on the campaign trail or introduced GOP hopefuls to crowds at rallies in states like Texas and New York.

It comes as Trump has been at the center of a major blending between sports and party politics in recent months.

The president has sought to capitalize on support from star athletes like New York Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart and 64-year-old former major league pitcher Roger Clemens as he rallies for GOP candidates across the country.

Several former athletes or sports figures are separately showing up on political tickets as GOP candidates, all of them backing Trump.

Former New York Yankees first baseman Mark Teixeira is running for U.S. House in Texas’s 21st Congressional District. Former NFL kicker Jay Feely is running for U.S. House in Arizona’s 1st Congressional District, and former sports broadcaster Michele Tafoya is running for U.S. Senate in Minnesota.

All of them have pledged support for the president while seeking to win their races.

Trump over the past year repeatedly has tapped into American sports culture in a bid to shore up support with his base, particularly in Southern states and among younger, male voters.

He’s attended several top-tier college football games in recent weeks, hosted the gold medal-winning U.S. men’s hockey team at this year’s State of the Union address and announced last week he would award the Presidential Medal of Freedom to Clemens, the pitcher who had introduced him moments earlier at a rally in Texas.

“Trump’s role in this cycle has been to be the energizer in chief. And if you’re trying to get people excited, athletes and coaches play the perfect role,” said Loretta Lepore, a Republican communications strategist who worked in the first Trump administration.

“These athletes have high name ID and are really accustomed to motivational type speeches that can create energy. And the party needs that right now. Plus, it makes sense thematically while we’re in the thrust of football season.”

The GOP’s gravitation toward sports figures comes as polls show support for the president slipping among younger and male voters, a key demographic that helped Trump win the White House in 2016 and 2024.

There is no guarantee such a strategy will pay off at the ballot box, some observers argue.

“For your average political figure, they’re really interested in the imagery associated with sports, but this is not what drives where the campaign checks are flowing,” said David Niven, a political scientist and researcher at the University of Cincinnati. “It probably gives them a good feeling about energy more than it drives any votes.”

Many political forecasters expect sweeping losses for the GOP on Nov. 3.

But candidates on the Republican ticket in the midterm cycle who come from sports backgrounds could have cause for optimism.

An analysis conducted by sports and politics researcher Tom Knecht found former athletes and coaches who have run for federal office the first time won more than 70 percent of the races they entered from 1936 to 2023, and of that group, about 58 percent were Republican.

Teixeira is running in a heavily Republican district, while Feely and Tafoya are expected to have tougher election fights. Recent polling shows Feely within a handful of percentage points behind his Democratic counterpart and Tafoya trailing by more than 5 points.

“I’ve found athletes have a pretty conservative bent in just about every sport except for basketball. And we know sports have a lot of cultural values that map pretty well onto the GOP like individualism, self-reliance and masculinity,” Knecht told The Hill.

“Yet it seems like the more important thing for them [the GOP this election cycle] is getting people out to the polls rather than changing their minds.”

The NFL surprised many in the sports gambling industry this week when it filed a petition with the Supreme Court urging it to clear a path for states to regulate prediction markets, which have broken into the sports gaming world in a big way. The NFL’s stance is a notable departure from the posture of other leagues, like MLB and the NHL, which in some cases have directly partnered with prediction market platforms. The Trump administration has signaled support for many of those companies in the wake of recent legal challenges they have faced from various state governments.

With an MLB lockout looming, Sen. Katie Britt (R-Ala.) highlighted an issue facing the Atlanta Braves, the de facto home club for many Southern states. Due to a tax law signed in 2021, the Braves are set to pay a new tax penalty, Britt said, “simply because they’re a publicly traded sports team.” Britt and Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.) this month introduced bipartisan legislation that would update the federal tax code to ensure publicly traded professional sports teams receive the same tax treatment as privately owned teams. The bill could get a vote during the coming Senate session after the midterms.

Legendary Chicago Bears head coach Mike Ditka died Friday. Ditka, 86, enjoyed a lengthy television career after he retired from coaching in the NFL and was outspoken on politics. A Republican, Ditka publicly supported President Trump as early as 2016 and said he was willing to stump for him at Republican conventions, though he was never invited to do so.

Jocks on the Hill: Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.)

Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.), the only current member of Congress to have hiked the entire Appalachian Trail, answered some sports questions for The Hill.

“It would have to be golf. I mean it’s actually hiking and mountaineering but you probably don’t consider that a sport. I’ve climbed hundreds of mountains and I spent a lot more time doing that than I do playing golf but in terms of traditional sport … close behind it was baseball which I LOVE but was sadly never very good at it.”

“Oh the Nats [MLB’s Washington Nationals] for sure, and that’s in the context that the Senators left when I was 8 years old, it broke my heart and they left again. So now I’m hangin’ on to the Nats for the rest of my life.”

Is there an athlete you admired growing up:

“In recent years it’s been Grant Hill more than anybody else. He’s just a wonderful athlete and community leader and father. I was very fond of Charlie Taylor when he was playing for the Redskins back in the day, too.”

Hate is a strong word, but is there a team you like to root against:

“Well, I mean … Dallas Cowboys. I’m a Washingtonian, ya know? In my older age I try to be respectful when they have talent but still … just no.”

Sports and politics are both full of cliches, is there one that resonates with you?

“Yeah, first loss is best loss. If things are going poorly in politics, shut it all, take the heat, get out of the inning, get out of the four down series just move on to the next one. It shows up in golf, too. When you miss that three-foot putt, you can’t think about it 30 seconds later it’s gotta be gone. Ya lost it, just move on.”

Sportico is out with a new story using a Freedom of Information Act request to lay out all the items the University of Michigan removed from disgraced former coach Sherrone Moore’s office after it fired him following his arrest last year. Among them were a wedding ring, a Bible, money, a police patch, four “OSU kill boards” and smelling salts.

With a new NHL season underway, the Los Angeles Times published a comprehensive long-form story marking 60 years of the Kings, a club that went from having 4,000 empty seats to being one of the league’s most valuable franchises today.

In case you missed Candace Buckner’s latest column from The Athletic, she pulls no punches writing about Sophie Cunningham, whom she says the Indiana Fever should cut to distance the franchise from her controversies, saying she’s “too turbulent to be paired with Caitlin Clark.”

articles.title: EXCLUSIVE: Inside LA's homeless hellscape — unlikely critics blast Dems as GOP hopeful tours Skid Row
articles.summary: Steve Hilton walked through Skid Row's homeless encampments, accusing California's Democratic leaders of fueling the crisis with billions in spending.
articles.body: LOS ANGELES — Surrounded by sprawling homeless encampments, drug use and trash-strewn sidewalks in the heart of Los Angeles' Skid Row, Republican gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton blasted California's homelessness crisis as a "political scandal," accusing Democratic leaders of spending billions in taxpayer dollars while allowing the streets to deteriorate. "'The homelessness crisis,' as if it's some kind of natural disaster that can't be helped," Hilton told Fox News Digital, referring to how politicians and others describe the conditions as he surveyed the sprawling encampments. "No, it is not a crisis. It's actually a scandal. It's a political scandal because the people in charge, they've caused this with their policies." Skid Row, the epicenter of California's homelessness crisis, is facing renewed scrutiny after a sweeping federal drug raid Thursday. The crackdown came as voting gets underway in the Nov. 3 governor's race, with Hilton challenging Democrat Xavier Becerra in a contest where homelessness and billions in taxpayer spending have emerged, yet again, as key campaign issues. HOUSING FIRST IS A DISASTER. I SAW SACRAMENTO'S HOMELESS CHAOS FIRSTHAND 'A real crony game' Fox News Digital observed sprawling homeless encampments, Narcan distribution points, human feces on sidewalks and piles of ash from what people in the neighborhood said were fires lit earlier that morning to keep warm. Hilton accused years of Democratic leadership of failing to solve California's homelessness problem despite billions in taxpayer spending, while taking aim at government-funded nonprofits and developers he claims have financially benefited from the crisis. "The real estate developers, and it's a real crony game now, which I've been told about many times," he continued. "We've got a small number of real estate developers who are in on this, and they get all the contracts to build these apartment units for people that don't help them at all, because the other part of it isn't being done in terms of drug addiction or whatever." TAXPAYER-FUNDED 'METH MANSION' UNDER FIRE AS CRIME CONCERNS MOUNT AROUND HOMELESS CAMPUS "The point about these nonprofits is that they're part of this philosophy, the ideology of harm reduction, all the things we've talked about, which means that they are not actually trying to solve the problem," Hilton said. "Because if they solve the problem, they don't get paid anymore. So they have an incentive to keep it going." In September, federal prosecutors charged the founder of a Los Angeles-area homelessness nonprofit with wire fraud, alleging he misused taxpayer funds, including nearly $50,000 for a trip to Tahiti, after receiving more than $118 million in public funding through government contracts. Federal and local authorities, including the FBI, DEA and LAPD, arrested 23 of 28 defendants charged in a sweeping drug trafficking investigation Thursday, targeting alleged gang-affiliated dealers and independent operators accused of selling fentanyl, methamphetamine and other drugs in and around Skid Row. Hilton argued that addressing homelessness begins with enforcing existing laws and removing encampments from California's streets. KAREN BASS GRILLED OVER BROKEN HOMELESSNESS PROMISE, BLAMES BUREAUCRACY FOR SLOWED PROGRESS "My plan is very simple. How we get clean streets in California. Number one, enforce the law, get people off the streets," he said. "Letting people live like this, and not just the people who live like this, but all the people who aren't living like this who have to experience this every single day. The collapse of civilized life in their city," Hilton said. "It's the opposite, it's cruel." 'I like being on drugs' As Hilton walked through Skid Row with Fox News Digital, one woman living on the streets offered a candid admission about her drug use. LA REAL ESTATE VET COMES AT MAYOR BASS WITH RECEIPTS OVER DAMNING HOMELESSNESS REPORT: 'SHE DOESN'T GET IT' "I like being on drugs, but if I have to quit, then I most definitely will," she told Hilton when he asked whether she wanted to stop using drugs. The woman, who said she had been living on Skid Row for five years, described moving to Los Angeles from Syracuse, New York, in part because she had heard about California's methadone clinics. She also said a former boyfriend had planned to find housing. "I heard about the methadone clinics," she explained, saying she wanted access to methadone treatment. Despite her admission about drug use, the woman said she was considering entering a treatment program in Tarzana, where she had heard patients could stay for a year or longer and receive methadone twice a day. STEVE HILTON LAUNCHES AD MOCKING XAVIER BECERRA'S '36 YEARS' AS A CAREER POLITICIAN IN CALIFORNIA GOV RACE Venus, a Skid Row volunteer who helps distribute food, blasted Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass over the handling of homelessness, even as Bass joined local law enforcement officials Thursday to announce the results of a sweeping drug crackdown in the neighborhood. "We all loved her from the beginning, but she lied about the homeless," Venus said, pointing to the conditions surrounding her on Skid Row. "What is going on, Mayor Bass? We voted for you." Venus later added, "She didn't do her job," and said Bass’ pledge was "getting rid of the homeless. She never did nothing. Nothing, nothing at all. Shame on her." Hilton also took aim at his Democratic opponent, Becerra, accusing the longtime politician of taking California voters for granted while failing to offer solutions to the state's mounting problems. "If you can't be bothered to earn people's vote, then you don't deserve people's votes. He's not campaigning. He's backing out of every single debate. I mean, I've never seen anything like it. It's complete contempt for the voters and for California," said Hilton. Hilton, a former Fox News host, argued that Californians are growing fed up with years of Democratic leadership, pointing to homelessness, high taxes and the soaring cost of living as reasons voters may be ready for a change. "I know everyone says, well, it's California, Republican can't win. I don't know. I think people are sick of all this," Hilton said. "And they're sick of Becerra just taking them for granted, and I think we can win this election." 'I'm a patriotic American communist' On Skid Row, Fox News Digital encountered criticism of Democratic leadership from an unlikely political perspective: a man who described himself as a "patriotic American communist." TRUMP ADMINISTRATION YANKS FUNDING FROM LA HOMELESS AGENCY AMID EXPLOSIVE FRAUD PROBE: 'NECESSARY STEP' The man, who identified himself as Adrian, said he had moved from Orange County and ended up on Skid Row following a medical incident. "I'm a patriotic American communist, part of the American Communist Party," Adrian said. Adrian said he belonged to the American Communist Party, distancing himself from the mainstream Democratic Party. Asked whether California's leaders were doing enough to address homelessness, Adrian was blunt. "Oh, definitely not. I have to be honest, I'm a leftist, and so the Democratic Party isn't for me. I'm more left than they are," he said. Adrian said he had been living on Skid Row for about a year after being evicted from a medical facility, and now volunteers at the Skid Row Care Campus, which he credited with providing therapy, medical services and community activities. Fox News Digital reached out to Becerra's campaign and Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass' office for comment.

articles.title: Secret Service chief says threats against protectees up 40%, cites internet and mental health
articles.summary: Secret Service Director Sean Curran and Deputy Director Matt Quinn gave their first joint interview with "60 Minutes" about the increased threats they face.
articles.body: Secret Service leadership detailed the "massive increase" in threats against the presidency and agents in the past year during a special joint interview with CBS' "60 Minutes" on Sunday. "It's like we've never seen before," Secret Service Director Sean Curran told host Norah O'Donnell. "The threats on our full-time protectees are up just over 40% than they were last year. That's a massive increase." Curran, along with Deputy Director Matt Quinn, were questioned as to what they believed caused the rise in threats. Curran suggested that the growth of the internet was a factor, but O'Donnell wondered if President Donald Trump also drove the threats. TRUMP HAS BECOME AMERICA'S MOST TARGETED LEADER, FACING THREATS EVERY FEW MONTHS "President Trump is one of the most polarizing political figures in American history. Is that in some way leading to the increase in these threats?" O'Donnell asked. "We are an apolitical organization. We're here to protect who we're sworn to protect," Curran answered. "Look, I would say there's people on both sides of the aisle that either love or hate any president. I think the biggest factor we're dealing with today is mental health issues for sure. And more people are being pushed over the edge in either direction," Quinn added. "The world is different than what it was 20 years ago. You know, social media changes people," Curran said. The men also did not clarify whether more threats came from left-wing or right-wing sources, explaining that they do not "weigh" threats in that way, citing concerns from both the Jan. 6 Capitol riots and the assassination attempts against Trump. 'DECOY' AIR FORCE ONE WAS PROTECTED BY US FIGHTER JETS, OFFICIAL SAYS Curran, who was the lead agent protecting Trump during the first assassination attempt against him in 2024, emphasized the importance of preparation. O'Donnell later connected this idea to the reports of Trump's Air Force One plane switch in August. "Look, that's not the first time we've done that. We wish that wasn't reported, 'cause that takes some of our tactics away from being able to do something similar again. Certainly wasn't the first time where we did something like that," Curran said, though he clarified that he did not say whether they had ever used a decoy plane prior to this incident. Quinn also defended the procedure which left agents behind in a decoy plane. "When you're operating in any protective detail with the president of the United States, for any president, the priority is the president. Everyone else, staff, agents, media, personnel involved are not the priority, including our own personnel. As hard as that may be for some to understand, the mission is to protect the president of the United States," Quinn said. I SERVED AS TRUMP’S NSA. SCOTUS NEED TO STOP COURTS PUTTING THE PRESIDENT'S SECURITY AT RISK Fox News Digital reached out to the White House for comment. This interview came as the Secret Service faces ongoing scrutiny after three officials were placed on leave in August. Protection for the president has also come under scrutiny as the FBI hesitates to release documents pertaining to the investigation of the assassination attempt on Trump at a rally in Butler, Pennsylvania. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Judicial Watch President Thomas Fitton, whose organization sued the Department of Justice for documents related to the event, criticized the slow process. "They are telling us that, at current processing rates, the process will take 12 years. Under the FBI's timeline, we won't even be able to challenge what they withheld until 12 years from now. That is obviously unacceptable, and I would like to know what leadership at the FBI and DOJ think about that position," Fitton told Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Senate Republican settles six-year-old campaign bill after being called out on social media
articles.summary: After the founder of Holly's Sweet Treats called out Sen. Roger Marshall's campaign for stiffing her company on a 2020 purchase, the debt was paid off.
articles.body: Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., paid a six-year-old campaign bill after a bakery owner called him out on social media for allegedly failing to pay for cookies and other treats ordered for a 2020 election watch party. Holly Thomas, a bakery founder, said in an Oct. 8 Facebook post that she would never vote for Marshall because his campaign had failed to pay a $678.75 bill despite her repeated attempts to collect the money. Thomas shared an image of the invoice and a photo that appeared to show custom cookies made for Marshall's campaign. "Do you know why I will never vote for Roger Marshall? Because six years ago, when I was a brand-new small business owner, his campaign ordered cookies and treats from my bakery for his primary election watch party. And I never got paid. For nearly a year, I made repeated attempts to collect payment, reaching out by phone and email. I never received a return phone call, and the invoice was never paid," Thomas wrote in the post. SLEEPER SENATE RACE EMERGES AS UNEXPECTED HEADACHE FOR REPUBLICANS AHEAD OF MIDTERMS "Not only was I just starting out, but we were also in the middle of COVID, when small businesses everywhere were struggling just to keep their doors open. Every single dollar mattered. Those cookies and treats cost money to make, employees' time to prepare, and resources that my little business couldn't afford to give away," she explained. "Six years later, I haven't forgotten. This isn't about political parties or policy disagreements. It's about my personal experience as a small business owner and the importance of honoring financial commitments. That experience is why Roger Marshall will never get my vote," Thomas concluded. Marshall — who had been serving in the U.S. House of Representatives when he won election to the U.S. Senate in 2020 — addressed the issue on Oct. 10, sharing a screenshot showing a $1,300 payment to the establishment. GOP SENATOR ALLEGES SCHUMER BEHIND 'HIT JOB' REPORT ON FORMER PATIENTS "As some folks may have seen, there was a post on social media regarding an unpaid 2020 cookie bill. We have absolutely no idea how this happened, but rest assured as soon as it became known to us, we immediately attempted to contact the business in order to apologize, and we have repaid the bill from 2020, double," Marshall's post on X noted. POWERFUL UNION LEADER BACKS REPUBLICAN IN KEY SENATE SHOWDOWN Thomas confirmed that the bill had been paid. "But I can officially confirm that Roger Marshall has paid his bill! Better late than never, right? Six years later, I guess we can finally mark that invoice PAID!" she wrote in part of a Facebook post. "Thank you all for the overwhelming support! Now, back to doing what I do best!" CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Marshall is seeking re-election this year.

articles.title: They helped undermine our institutions — do they see the consequences yet?
articles.summary: Institutions built to resolve constitutional crises are only as strong as the trust people place in them. So what happens when the media actively work to undermine them?
articles.body:
Certain members of media are apparently only now discovering the cost of undermining the institutions that protect civil society from unrest and collapse.

MS NOW host Stephanie Ruhle and longtime CNN correspondent Dana Bash wondered recently whether the institutions that adjudicate electoral matters will “hold” if the November midterms produce a crisis.

“When we in the news are covering these elections,” said Ruhle , “when we say we could be on the verge of a potential constitutional crisis, lots of people blow it off. They’re like, ‘Oh my gosh, that’s crazy. Our institutions always hold. This is the United States of America.’ Are you that confident?”

Responded Bash, “I’m hopeful. I’ll use that word. And that is because so far, the institutions have held. But we have seen them bending almost to the point where they break.”

She added, “So, it is something that I cover — I know you cover on a daily basis — watching for signs that the system might not hold or that the system might be challenged by the most important person in this country as people go to the polls. And the fact that we are all hyper aware and vigilant of it is half the battle, I do think. … And so I’m going to go back to hopeful. I don’t — I’m not going to say confident. I just want to stick with hopeful.”

Surely, they understand that institutions built to resolve constitutional crises are only as strong as the trust people place in them.

If they understand this, then they might consider the damage their own industry has done by attempting to destroy the legitimacy of those institutions — above all the Supreme Court — simply because some of its decisions do not align fully with Democratic policy preferences.

The attacks on the court, from CNN, MS NOW, and elsewhere, are especially egregious. They are also especially relevant here. When we talk about institutions designed to guide us through constitutional crises, the Supreme Court is obviously at the top of the list. But in the popular press, the court is treated as illegitimate, described as severely right-wing and in the pocket of Republicans and their donors.

A cursory review of the court’s actual record shows it is none of these things. Since Trump’s reelection, he has won three merits decisions on executive authority and lost two. On the emergency docket, there have been 43 applications thus far (four withdrawn and one pending), 41 of which were filed by the administration, according to Ballotpedia . Of the decided applications, about two-thirds favor the White House. A closer look, however, shows the court less often expanding executive power than reining in lower-court judges who had badly overstepped their authority .

The court might be best described as a “mixed bag.” It has not sided with activist judges, but neither has it rubber-stamped Trump’s executive overreaches or upheld his most treasured initiatives.

The facts, however, have not prevented the media from waging a counterprogramming and subversion campaign against the court’s legitimacy, simply because it has a conservative majority.

At CNN, supposedly the more serious network, legal analyst Jeffrey Toobin referred to the Supreme Court as Republican Sen. Mitch “ McConnell’s Supreme Court .” Chief Supreme Court analyst Joan Biskupic — doing the “people say” routine of stating her opinion without stating her opinion — worried that the public sees the majority as “ very politically motivated ” and accused it of “plowing through all sorts of norms, rolling back a half century of abortion rights and also changing gun rights, changing regulatory authority. Doing all these things based on patterns that arise from their private partisan roots.” Chief legal affairs correspondent Paula Reid alleged that the “conservative supermajority” holds “ an increasingly expansive view of executive power .”

Journalist and commentator Fareed Zakaria also warned that the court “has been growing more ideologically predictable — that is, politically partisan – in recent years,” and that judges “ appointed by Republicans now almost always rule in ways that Republicans want them to .”

It bears repeating that this is the exact opposite of the truth. No liberal justice crossed over to join the conservative majority in any of the executive-authority merits cases the Trump administration won in its second term. And when the White House lost, it was always because conservative justices joined their liberal colleagues in decisions that were 5-4, 6-3, and even 7-2.

This follows a long tradition, which continues through to this day, of Republican-appointed justices being less ideologically rigid, crossing over to vote with their liberal counterparts, even though the liberals almost never do this.

At MS NOW, a network created for histrionic liberals, the coverage is only slightly more deranged: The court is “ illegitimate ,” “ rogue ,” and “ captured .” It comprises “ six right wing politicians in robes ,” “ a kind of unaccountable super-legislature .” The “ court itself is rigged ,” composed of “ partisan hacks .” It is a “ partisan institution full of hacks that will do everything in their power to protect Donald Trump .” And so on, and so forth.

A campaign by major media, including the New York Times and ProPublica, tried to make audiences care which flags Justice Sam Alito’s wife flies outside their vacation home . So determined were they to cast aspersions on the justice that they demonized a beloved flag of the American Revolutionary era in the process — a flag that liberals and conservatives alike had flown up to that point for decades without any partisan connotation.

Almost nothing said or insinuated by any of these media figures about the justices or the court is true, yet the attacks continue anyway. No mind is ever given to the long-term damage that their slanders cause to the institutions that will be counted on to hold our country together in any dispute over our laws and elections.

It’s a fairly simple lesson, yet one apparently lost on single-minded news organizations run by wannabe resistance fighters.

Becket Adams is a journalist and media critic in Washington.

articles.title: Americans clash over Supreme Court expansion as fight over 9 justices heats up: ‘Let’s pack it now’
articles.summary: Americans on Capitol Hill share divided views on SCOTUS expansion, court packing, and term limits as lawmakers debate the Supreme Court's future.
articles.body: As lawmakers spar over whether to expand the U.S. Supreme Court beyond nine justices, Americans interviewed by Fox News Digital on Capitol Hill had competing views on whether the nation's highest court needs a shake-up at all. "If it's not broken, don't fix it," Tim from Washington, D.C., told Fox News Digital. "If you had more justices, you could have more differing opinions there," Derek, also from Washington, said. "So you'd have to have more of a consensus on whatever they're voting on." The debate comes after a Republican-backed constitutional amendment to permanently fix the court at nine justices failed in the House in September, falling short of the two-thirds majority required for passage. MORNING GLORY: DSA DEMOCRATS' RADICAL PLAN TO RESHAPE AMERICA STARTS WITH THE SUPREME COURT Democratic lawmakers have also introduced proposals to reshape the court, including legislation to expand its membership, establish term limits and impose additional ethics requirements. " If we're gonna change the size, we need to do it now," said Carl from Texas. "If you're going to pack the court, let's pack it now." One person Fox News Digital spoke with questioned the motives behind efforts to increase the number of justices. "I think those who want to increase the size, maybe just have a bias to it, if it be Republican or Democrat," Tim said about the idea of expanding the number of justices. "I say just leave it as it is, man." JOHN YOO: THE LEFT'S SUPREME COURT PANIC COLLAPSES UNDER THE WEIGHT OF THE FACTS Democrats have become increasingly angry over many of the court’s votes, and many have alleged their rulings to be rooted in politics rather than law. "The more people weigh in, the more accurate the results would be, right?" an interviewee said. One also argued that while he would be in favor of potentially expanding the Supreme Court, it would be dependent on how many additional justices were to be added. "It depends on how much more they add," Derek said. "One or two more doesn't seem like it's that much, but if they're like, ‘Double it.’ Well, starting to just kind of go overboard at that point." REPUBLICANS SOUND ALARM OVER HIDDEN MIDTERM STAKES THAT COULD RESHAPE SUPREME COURT FOR DECADES Several proposals by Democrats have been introduced to reshape the court, including legislation from Rep. Al Green, D-Texas, to expand the bench from nine to 13 justices, and a separate measure from Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., to establish 18-year terms of active service for newly appointed justices. "I think that more substantial change would be putting in term limits," Mark from Washington, D.C., said. "The size would allow for the next several presidents to appoint more people. I don't know that it changes the political bent of the current situation, whereas a term limits might be more effective." Other Democratic proposals would impose enforceable ethics standards and require greater transparency surrounding the court's emergency rulings, often referred to as its "shadow docket." Republicans argue Democrats’ proposals to overhaul the Supreme Court are a reaction to the party’s anger at rulings not being in their favor. LIBERAL JUSTICE HAMMERS SUPREME COURT FOR FAST-TRACKING EMERGENCY DOCKET CASES House Republicans sought to permanently cap the court at nine justices, casting their proposed constitutional amendment to reject Democratic efforts to expand the court. It failed to secure the required two-thirds majority needed to pass the House. Amending the Constitution would then also require a two-thirds majority vote in the Senate and then ratification by three-fourths of the states. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Article III, Section 1 of the Constitution establishes the Supreme Court but does not specify how many justices should serve on it, leaving Congress with the authority to determine its size. Congress initially established six seats under the Judiciary Act of 1789. The court's size changed several times throughout the 19th century, reaching as many as 10 justices before Congress established the current nine-justice structure in 1869.

articles.title: Trump's backyard is quietly transforming into 'Silicon Valley South' as wealthy Americans flock in
articles.summary: Palm Beach is drawing tech giants and Wall Street executives, says real estate expert Margit Brandt, who compares the region to Silicon Valley.
articles.body: A wealthy Southern enclave once known as a playground for retirees and snowbirds is transforming into a growing technology and financial hub, drawing comparisons to Silicon Valley as businesses, Wall Street executives and entrepreneurs move in. Palm Beach County, Florida, is attracting new attention as wealthy Americans seek alternatives to high-tax states like New York and California. "Palm Beach has changed from a place where people come to retire to a place that people come to build," luxury real estate expert Margit Brandt told Fox News Digital. "There's been countless CEOs and major heads of companies that have moved their businesses to Palm Beach," she said, pointing to Florida's favorable tax climate and lifestyle as major draws. THE RED STATES RACING AHEAD IN AMERICA’S POWERFUL WEALTH BOOM — AND THE STATES FALLING BEHIND The region is also home to President Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago estate, often dubbed the "Southern White House," placing the emerging business hub in the backyard of one of the country's most recognizable political landmarks. The shift comes amid changing migration patterns across the country, with Internal Revenue Service data for 2022–2023 showing taxpayer losses across numerous California and Northeastern counties, while much of the Southeast recorded gains. Brandt believes Palm Beach County could become a major technology hub, citing its room for expansion as an advantage over more densely developed destinations. "We have tons of room to grow," she said, pointing to areas like Wellington and western Palm Beach County where new schools, hospitals and infrastructure could accommodate additional businesses and families. The region is also attracting technology investment alongside its established financial services industry. In September 2025, California-based software company ServiceNow announced plans to establish a regional innovation hub and artificial intelligence institute in West Palm Beach. AMERICANS KEEP MOVING TO TEXAS AND FLORIDA — BUT ONE OTHER RED STATE IS GROWING EVEN FASTER The expansion is projected to generate $1.8 billion in economic impact and create more than 850 jobs over five years, according to the company. ServiceNow also committed to occupying up to 200,000 square feet of office space at 10 CityPlace, a development by billionaire real estate investor Stephen Ross's Related Ross. "The tech has particularly been exciting for Palm Beach County," Brandt said. Meanwhile, Palm Beach County's population reached an estimated 1.58 million residents in July 2025, an increase of 5.6% since April 2020, according to the U.S. Census Bureau. Brandt said new office developments in West Palm Beach and Palm Beach Gardens have made it easier for companies to establish a presence in the region. "Florida has just been a really easy landing place," she said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Beyond business opportunities, Brandt pointed to year-round outdoor activities, warm weather and family life as major attractions for newcomers. For Brandt, the region's evolution is far from complete. "Palm Beach County, I think we're like in beginning stages of what's possible here," she said.

articles.title: Graham, Andrews face off as GOP jitters grow in South Carolina
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ Debate night in South Carolina ▪ Russia deal faces backlash ▪ DOJ investigating news outlets ▪ Mike Johnson’s uncertain future Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) and her Democratic opponent Annie Andrews went head-to-head Sunday night for their first and likely only debate in a contest that favors the GOP but looks increasingly…
articles.body:
Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) and her Democratic opponent Annie Andrews went head-to-head Sunday night for their first and likely only debate in a contest that favors the GOP but looks increasingly gettable for Democrats.

Democrats haven’t won statewide in South Carolina in 20 years, and Graham has led in polling, unlike GOP candidates in some typically red states in what may be a “blue wave” election.

But the dynamic has changed from how the race was expected to go since the sudden death of Graham’s brother, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), in July. Instead of facing a longtime incumbent who’s had years to build up his reputation and experience, Democrats now face his sister, who was appointed to the seat three months ago and has faced criticism — including from members of her own party — that she’s too inexperienced for the role.

“She has shown time and time again that she is not up for the job,” Andrews said Sunday night.

Graham defended herself as qualified for the position, pointing to the work she has already done as a senator.

“I’ve been in the Senate for three months now. I’ve already co-sponsored several bills that protect farmers, that protect the American taxpayer,” she said.

Graham also defended herself over a memorable gaffe that she made during a primary runoff debate in August against Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.). Responding to a question about whether the U.S. would have the responsibility to defend Taiwan from a hypothetical Chinese invasion, Graham said she’s “not that informed” on national security.

“At least I’m honest. If I don’t know something, I am glad to say it, and I’ll say it again tonight. But … you are deceiving the people of South Carolina,” Graham shot back at Andrews.

She successfully avoided any similar gaffes during her faceoff with Andrews, though the Democratic nominee continued to press her over her limited experience, accusing her of trying to ride the coattails of her brother’s name.

Graham sought to tie Andrews to the most far-left factions of her party.

“Annie Andrews will not stand up to the Socialist Democratic Party. She’s only going to join them,” she said, criticizing the response from some progressives to Hamas’s Oct. 7, 2023, attack.

The event seems likely to be the only time that Graham and Andrews will meet on the debate stage. Andrews pressed Graham a few times during the debate to commit to additional meetings, but Graham rebuffed her, saying she wants to focus on interacting with voters.

Although the race still favors the GOP, there’s some signs it may be tighter than initially expected.

A few surveys from Republican-leaning pollsters have shown Graham only a few points ahead, putting Andrews within the margin of error.

The election handicapper Cook Political Report shifted its rating of the race from “solid Republican” to “likely Republican” late last month.

Decision Desk HQ rates the race as “lean Republican,” giving Graham a 70 percent chance of winning. That’s down from close to 80 percent about a month ago.

Senate Leadership Fund, the main Senate Republican super PAC, is directing $5 million into the contest as an “insurance policy,” another sign of the GOP feeling some jitters. That money may be helpful, as Andrews has been outraising and outspending Graham and constantly appearing in ads.

National Democrats have yet to invest in the race, instead ramping up spending in states like Kansas and Iowa.

The Hill’s Sudiksha Kochi has a helpful rundown of what else to expect this week in key House and Senate races, as we’re three weeks out from Election Day. Sign up for The Hill Insider here to get “This week on the Hill” every Monday.

On top of more high-profile debates, President Trump is visiting Ohio today and Alaska on Tuesday to boost two potentially vulnerable GOP incumbents, Sens. Jon Husted and Dan Sullivan , respectively.

▪ The Hill : Five takeaways from testy South Carolina debate.

▪ The Hill : The Senate races most likely to flip.

A federal judge told the Trump administration that its taxpayer-funded ads are likely unlawful and must stop immediately. The Department of Homeland Security had said the ad campaign was set to conclude on Sunday. The president has said he would fund the ads through political contributions going forward.

The president and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are considering firing U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle following reports that she sought money from a GOP donor to pay off her debts during her confirmation process, a senior U.S. official told The Associated Press . The source said a decision will likely be made this week.

A terminal at the international airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, was struck again by a projectile a day after a strike that killed 12 people and injured 300 others. The Iran-backed Houthis have claimed responsibility for both attacks. The airport has been hit four times over the course of five days.

A rescue worker puts out a fire at residential houses destroyed in a Russian strike on Kharkiv, Ukraine, on Oct. 11, 2026. (AP Photo/Andrii Marienko)

SHAKY GROUND : There’s already growing skepticism about the president’s announcement Sunday that Russia and Ukraine agreed to an “energy ceasefire” in their war, as Moscow soon after struck a Ukrainian power plant.

In a Truth Social post early Sunday, Trump said both parties had agreed to the deal and that it would take effect immediately.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said in a post on the social platform X that his country supports the ceasefire but was waiting for more details from the U.S. as Russia must agree to it as well. A source close to Zelensky told CNN that Trump’s announcement took him by surprise.

But soon after, Zelensky said a power plant in Kharkiv was attacked and Ukrainian skies had been “infested” with Russia attacks all day.

“Ukraine wants peace. The question is whether Russia does,” Zelensky said.

Trump has pointed to the war between Russia and Ukraine as the central cause of rising energy costs in the U.S., downplaying the role of the Iran war.

He announced a deal Friday for the U.S. to purchase diesel fuel from Russia to address the high energy costs, spurromg bipartisan backlash from lawmakers who say the deal is providing a financial lifeline to Russia.

A group on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee argue it violates a ban on Russian energy imports that Congress passed in 2022 to prevent U.S. dollars from supporting Russia’s invasion.

Zelensky called the deal a “birthday gift” for Russian President Vladimir Putin .

▪ The Hill : GOP lawmaker to introduce bill to block purchase.

▪ The Hill : Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) says deal is ‘tarnishing’ Graham’s efforts.

RAMPING UP : The Trump administration’s standoff with the five major networks that make up the White House television pool has escalated further as the Department of Justice (DOJ) is reportedly investigating the outlets.

Six people familiar told The New York Times that the probe concerns whether antitrust laws were violated when the group — ABC, NBC, CBS, CNN and Fox News — briefly suspended their pool coverage of the president. They restored their coverage after a federal judge ordered the White House to allow CNN, MS NOW and Politico back onto the building’s grounds.

The sources told the Times that DOJ officials contacted the networks Friday, demanding communications and materials related to the pool.

“Group boycotts among commercial competitors can violate the Sherman Act,” a DOJ spokesperson told the outlet. “The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these news organizations have violated the antitrust laws.”

The opening of the probe comes as U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly , a Trump appointee who has been overseeing the case from the three outlets challenging the administration’s ban, is expected to issue a final ruling in the case by Tuesday.

▪ The New York Times : Why a court order didn’t stop Trump from keeping reporters off Air Force One.

STORM’S WAKE : Hurricane Isaias has been downgraded in intensity to a post-tropical storm and finished sweeping through the eastern U.S.

At least four deaths have been linked to Isaias , the first hurricane to form of this year’s Atlantic hurricane season. The storm made landfall near Destin, Fla., not far from Pensacola, on Friday evening as a Category 2 hurricane before moving into Alabama and continuing northeast, eventually going out to sea.

About 900,000 power outages were reported soon after the storm made landfall. About 170,000 homes remain without power in Florida and Alabama, according to poweroutage.us .

Officials are still reviewing the full extent of the damage.

▪ NewsNation : Victim’s husband recounts experience.

▪ Fox News : Hurricane’s devastating aftermath comes into focus.

The president will travel to Youngstown, Ohio, to deliver remarks at 7 p.m. He will then return to the White House.

Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) speaks with reporters outside of his office on Capitol Hill, on Sept. 16, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Mariam Zuhaib )

FATE UNCERTAIN : House Speaker Mike Johnson ‘s (R-La.) political career seems in doubt as he raised the possibility of leaving Congress if Republicans lose the lower chamber in November.

“Heaven forbid, if we lose this majority or whatever, I don’t know what my next chapter of life is,” Johnson told Fox News in an interview last week.

“If God moves on our hearts and says we should, you know, go back to my hometown of Shreveport and start a lawn business, I’ll do that with equal fervor. I mean, I just want to be of my highest and best use to God and to my country,” he continued.

The comments sparked enough chatter that Johnson’s spokesperson, Lance Trover , dismissed speculation that the Speaker would leave.

But some lawmakers and aides told The Hill’s Sudiksha Kochi that a push to choose a new leader for the House GOP is possible if the party suffers major losses next month.

“I think Mike could have done a better job, but it wasn’t just him,” one House member said. “It’s the whole leadership team.”

Democrats have been increasingly favored to win back control of the House as Election Day has approached. Decision Desk HQ’s forecast model currently gives the party a 76 percent chance to win the majority.

Part of that shift has come as Democrats have expanded their lead in the generic congressional ballot.

The Hill’s Mike Lillis reports that the landscape for House Republicans is growing bleaker by the day, noting that top election analysts have shifted more and more projections in Democrats’ favor in recent weeks.

“Republicans holding on to the House would be a shock given where the overall numbers are,” said Kyle Kondik , the managing editor of Sabato’s Crystal Ball, an independent election handicapper based at the University of Virginia.

▪ The Hill : Why North Carolina is shifting Democratic.

▪ The Hill : Trump continues red state campaign swing.

Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas receives Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis upon his arrival in the West Bank city of Ramallah on Dec. 22, 2025. (AP Photo/Nasser Nasser)

TRY AGAIN NEXT YEAR : Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas has postponed what was scheduled to be the first Palestinian elections in almost 20 years, illustrating the tensions within the West Bank and with Israel.

The elections were set to take place next month, but Abbas pushed them back to next September, also scheduling a presidential election for the same day.

The Palestinian Authority (PA), led by Abbas’s Fatah party for the past 20 years, administers parts of the West Bank under the terms of treaties signed between Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO). Abbas was first elected president in 2005, and his term has been extended indefinitely, with elections repeatedly being postponed.

While Fatah has remained in charge of the PA, the party has increasingly become more unpopular, with many Palestinians viewing it as corrupt.

The PLO’s executive committee said in a statement that conditions in East Jerusalem, the West Bank and the Gaza Strip aren’t conducive to holding elections and that Israel has not allowed election materials or international observers to enter Gaza.

Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar said in a post on X that Abbas was attempting to “drag Israel into this.” He called the statement a “ridiculous lie designed to evade responsibility and accountability.”

The decision had been expected as Palestinian factions met in Cairo to discuss delaying the vote, an official for the group Islamic Jihad told The Associated Press. Still, it raises further credibility issues for the PA with Palestinians and the international community.

The U.S.-brokered ceasefire between Israel and Hamas reached last year outlined some role for the PA, but it was mostly left undefined.

▪ The Associated Press : Progress stalls on the ceasefire.

Lethal injection is no kinder than a firing squad , Megan McArdle writes in The Washington Post.

The ‘scientific’ socialism of Abdul El-Sayed , Allysia Finley writes in The Wall Street Journal.

Reporters raise hands to question Vice President Vance, as he speaks with reporters in the James Brady Press Briefing Room at the White House on Sept. 3, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Alex Brandon )

And finally … Kat ie Zacharia , the president’s choice to be his next press secretary after Karoline Leavitt , will step behind the podium in the White House briefing room for the first time Tuesday.

Trump said in a post on Truth Social that Zacharia will start her tenure as White House press secretary today and will do an “introductory” news conference at 9:30 a.m. Tuesday. Zacharia is a lawyer and conservative commentator who served a brief stint as a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security earlier this year.

“Katie has been with me, in spirit, from the very beginning, and will do a fantastic job!” Trump said.

Leavitt left her role as press secretary in late August, shortly after returning from maternity leave for her second child. The position had been vacant since then.

A rotating group of members of the administration have conducted press briefings in her absence, though the last one was held by Attorney General Todd Blanche almost a month ago.
