articles.title: Pope Leo is asking the question AI can’t answer
articles.summary: Pope Leo isn’t asking us to reject progress. He is reminding us to define progress correctly.
articles.body:
Pope Leo XIV has just given America something it desperately needs in the artificial intelligence debate: a reason to slow down and think about the human being at the center of it.

On Monday, while flying back to Rome after his visit to France, the pope was asked about growing concerns that artificial intelligence could pose serious risks to humanity. His response was striking. He said those concerns, raised by AI experts, should be taken seriously. He rejected the idea that such warnings are simply “ fake news. “

Just days earlier, speaking in Paris, Leo had warned that technological development must remain at the service of the human person. He cautioned that our ideas and relationships can be impoverished by dehumanization and questioned what happens when human beings are judged primarily by efficiency and productivity.

I am excited about artificial intelligence. That may sound strange given what Pope Leo has been saying about the technology, but I think that is exactly why his message has caught my attention.

AI could make our lives better in ways we are only beginning to understand. It can help us work faster, discover new medicines, learn new skills and solve problems that once seemed impossible. I am not interested in pretending technological innovation is the enemy. Neither am I interested in putting the brakes on free markets simply because a new technology makes us uncomfortable.

But there is a question I increasingly find myself asking: What happens to us?

That is what I think Leo is bringing into the AI conversation. As politicians, businesses and technology leaders focus on what artificial intelligence can accomplish, the pope is asking us to remember the person standing on the other side of the technology.

What will it feel like to be human when AI can do most of the thinking for us? What happens when someone who is lonely, depressed or struggling with a personal problem stops calling a friend, family member or pastor and instead turns to a machine that is available 24 hours a day?

And perhaps most importantly, what happens to the dignity of work when machines can perform more and more of the tasks that once gave people not only a paycheck, but a sense of purpose?

Those questions aren’t arguments against AI. They are arguments for remembering why progress matters in the first place. I think conservatives should pay particular attention to that distinction.

Conservatives have traditionally understood that human beings are more than economic units. Work matters, but so do family, faith, community, responsibility and the relationships that give our lives meaning. Markets are incredibly powerful because they allow people to create, exchange and innovate. But markets cannot answer every question about what makes a society worth living in.

Neither can technology. We can create a machine that makes a decision faster than a human being. That doesn’t necessarily mean the machine should make every decision.

We can create an AI system that gives us an answer instantly. That doesn’t mean we should stop learning how to think.

We can create a chatbot that never gets tired of listening to us. That doesn’t mean it can replace the experience of sitting across from another human being who knows us, loves us and can tell us when we’re wrong.

And we can automate more work. But eventually we will have to confront a question that economics alone cannot answer: If a machine can do the work, what will give the human being dignity?

That is why Pope Leo’s message strikes me as bigger than an argument about artificial intelligence. He is showing us a different way to approach technological change: Put humanity first. That principle should not belong to the political left or the political right. It should be a starting point for anyone making decisions about the future of our country.

Before Washington asks what government can do with AI, we should ask what AI is doing to the people government is supposed to serve. Before corporations ask how much more productive AI can make their workers, they should also think about what happens to workers when productivity becomes the only measure of their value.

Before we celebrate machines becoming better at thinking, we should make sure we are still teaching human beings how to think. And before we allow technology to mediate more of our relationships, we should ask whether we are strengthening the human relationships that technology cannot replace.

None of this requires fear of the future. In fact, it requires confidence in humanity. I want my children to inherit a country where technology gives them more opportunities, not fewer. I want them to have access to tools that allow them to accomplish things that previous generations could only dream about. But I also want them to know that their worth isn’t determined by how productive they are. I want them to understand that a good life isn’t simply about being efficient.

Sometimes the most important things we do are inefficient. Raising a child is inefficient. Caring for an elderly parent is inefficient. Sitting with a friend who is hurting is inefficient. Going to church, having dinner with your family, mentoring a young person or simply listening to someone who needs to be heard may not show up neatly on a productivity chart. But these are precisely the things that make us human.

A society should not measure success solely by how quickly its machines can work, how much money its technology can generate or how many human tasks it can eliminate. We should also ask whether people have more freedom, more purpose, stronger families, deeper relationships and greater opportunities to live meaningful lives. Technology and markets should serve humanity.

That is why Pope Leo’s approach to AI deserves attention. He isn’t asking us to reject progress. He is reminding us to define progress correctly.

David Sypher Jr. is a freelance writer and commentator based in New Jersey.

articles.title: Federal agents raid Ilhan Omar’s DC home amid immigration fraud investigation
articles.summary: Rep. Ilhan Omar's home was the subject of a pre-dawn HSI raid.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE: The home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn, was raided early Monday morning by Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), a source familiar with the matter told Fox News Digital. Multiple federal agents with HSI jackets were seen outside Omar's Washington, D.C. home in the early hours of Monday. Two sources close to the investigation say the search stems from a criminal fraud investigation into the Somali-born congresswoman's immigration paperwork, which was filled out by her late father when she was a child. OMAR'S GOP CHALLENGER COMES OUT FIRING WITH VOW TO CLEAN UP 'MESS' IN DEEP BLUE DISTRICT: 'PEOPLE ARE FED UP' The raid of the Somali-born congresswoman's home started around 6 a.m. with HSI and Department of Homeland Security (DHS) leading the operation. The Department of Justice (DOJ) is also involved in the investigation. "Today in the Washington, D.C., area, Homeland Security Investigations executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the Department of Justice. This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal investigation," a DOJ spokesperson told Fox News Digital. The DOJ later added that the investigation was "criminal" in nature. articles.title: Johnson says he intends to stay on as GOP leader if Republicans lose majority
articles.summary: House Speaker Mike Johnson said last week that he could start a lawn business if the GOP loses the House majority, which he told CBS News' Robert Costa was "...
articles.body:
House Speaker Mike Johnson said he intends to serve as GOP leader if Republicans lose their House majority in November — but he remains bullish about the party's chances despite significant headwinds.

"In the unlikely scenario where we lost the majority, I would expect my colleagues would ask me to continue leading this conference, even if we have divided government," Johnson told CBS News' Robert Costa in an interview near Johnson's hometown of Shreveport, Louisiana.

Johnson, who has led House Republicans as speaker since 2023, has repeatedly pushed back on questions about his plans if the GOP loses the majority in the lower chamber in November. Known for his optimistic outlook, the speaker has expressed confidence that Republicans will hold on to the chamber, or even grow their narrow majority. But midterm dynamics traditionally boost the party opposing the party in control of the White House, and the unpopular war in Iran, high gas and diesel prices and other controversial Trump administration policies have added to those challenges for the GOP.

Last week, a comment Johnson made to Fox News on his plans for his future fueled speculation that he could retire from politics, as he suggested that he could go back to his hometown of Shreveport and start a lawn business if the GOP loses the House majority.

"It's just hilarious," Johnson said of the interest the comment spurred, telling Costa that the remark was "tongue in cheek."

"What I was trying to say to them is that throughout my whole life, my number one objective is to be of my highest and best use to God and to my country, and that's always what I've thought," Johnson said. "And I was trying to make the point that if God has a different design, then we'll follow that. But what I believe is, I'm going to be the speaker of the House for at least two more years."

But Johnson added, "If, heaven forbid, we lost the majority, I would expect my colleagues would call upon me to continue to lead the conference in divided government."

"My intention is to stay and serve, and that's what I've been doing, as best I can," he said.

Johnson has been campaigning heavily in recent weeks, with plans to hit 40 districts in 22 states before polls close on Election Day. He made a case for his continued leadership — whether in the majority or the minority — pointing to the millions of dollars he's brought in for Republicans this cycle, his busy travel schedule, and his work to corral a sometimes volatile GOP majority in this Congress.

"I'm not sure what the case would be for any alternative," he said. "I intend to stay and lead."

When pressed by Costa on whether he has it in him to be a tough, combative minority leader in the current political environment, Johnson pointed to his time on the House Judiciary Committee and his defense of President Trump during his two impeachment trials.

"I was a litigator in my past life — constitutional law attorney. We can be tough, but we can be happy warriors," he said. "That's what Ronald Reagan was. That's what I fashioned myself as."

But Johnson was clear: he has "no intention other than winning this majority and serving as speaker."

"That is what's going to happen," Johnson said. "And I'm telling you, I'm leaving it all in the field to do it."

articles.title: Schumer: Judge halting Trump ads ‘only the beginning’

articles.body:
Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) on Sunday hailed the order from a federal judge blocking the Trump administration from using taxpayer money to pay for advertisements promoting his leadership and pledged it marked “only the beginning” of a legal battle over the controversial ads.

“Taxpayer dollars are not Trump’s personal propaganda fund. This court order is a win for taxpayers, but stopping the ads is only the beginning,” Schumer said in a statement.

“Americans deserve answers about every dollar spent. That’s why I’ve demanded a thorough investigation into these ads and that all records are preserved,” he continued. “Now we need answers: who approved them, how much was spent, and who will be held accountable.”

The New York Times reported earlier this month that Trump personally ordered his budget director to use taxpayer money for the positive TV advertising campaign.

The administration created more than a dozen campaign-style ads paid for with taxpayer money to promote the president and echo his political rhetoric a few weeks before the midterm election.

Trump said on his Truth Social platform that he viewed the ads as “promotion for our Great U.S.” but last week announced they would be funded by his super PAC and no longer paid for by the U.S. government.

One ad closely resembled an online promotion the president posted to his Truth Social account in January 2024, as he was gearing up for his presidential campaign.

The ad from the 2024 election year urged supporters to text “TRUMP” to a phone number to support his campaign.

The more recent ad paid for by taxpayers did not include a fundraising pitch but was otherwise nearly identical.

It features Trump walking down a hallway accompanied by the soundtrack of a rousing speech he delivered at an unidentified event, declaring: “This is the final battle. With you at my side, we will demolish the deep state, we will expel the warmongers from our government.”

Several Republican senators warned it would be inappropriate to use taxpayer money to fund advertisements that closely resembled political ads.

“It’s a great message. I like the message, but it shouldn’t be paid for by taxpayer dollars,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) told reporters last month.

Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) said he wouldn’t think of using taxpayer money to fund political advertisements so close to an election.

“It would not have been something that I would have done,” he noted. “I know that the White House is not covered by the same guidance that we are, but it’s not something I would have done.”

articles.body: In one of the most hotly contested governor's races in the country, the Democratic nominee has been working overtime to cultivate a moderate image — while reportedly attending a church that openly embraces some of the progressive causes dividing voters in Iowa. Rob Sand, Iowa’s state auditor and its Democratic nominee for governor, regularly attended Plymouth Congregational United Church of Christ, located in the state’s capital, as of late 2025, according to a local journalist. Over the years, Plymouth has hosted and promoted drag queen performances, invited a transgender pastor to serve as a guest pastor and openly supported abortion. Sand has emphasized his faith on the campaign trail, repeatedly referencing Christianity and quoting scripture, at times successfully appealing to otherwise conservative Iowans. In addition to leaning on his faith, Sand has repeatedly described himself as independently minded, claimed to have voted for Republicans in the past and said that he sometimes prefers working with the GOP over Democrats, calling political parties "poison." "I am a Christian. I’m a conservative. But I’m not a party-based person," one voter is quoted as saying in a Sand press release. "I like to vote for the person as opposed to the party. And to me, (Sand) just seems really honest and down to earth. And I enjoyed him." IOWA GUBERNATORIAL HOPEFUL ZACH LAHN TELLS 'RUTHLESS' DEMOCRATS ARE HIDING THEIR BAD POLICIES Sand's reported church attendance, however, connects him to a congregation whose progressive religious and political positions stand in contrast to the moderate image he has emphasized on the campaign trail. Sand’s church is open about its progressive slant, with its "about" page featuring an image of churchgoers at a gay pride parade, noting that the church does not take the Bible literally and stating that it "has been an LGBTQ+ Open and Affirming congregation for more than 30 years." An image of the church included in a profile compiled by the United Church of Christ shows it flying a pride flag on its grounds, noting that the church "is a progressive powerhouse in the region." "Rob Sand goes to church weekly and does so in Iowa, unlike Zach Lahn. Rob’s faith is deeply important to him, and like many, he has never found a church where he agrees with everything, but does prefer traditional services with liturgy and classic hymns," a spokeswoman for his campaign told Fox News Digital. "Rob has always been independent-minded, and he isn’t going to take lessons in morality from a sex toy salesman who lives in Kansas." The mention of sex toys was a reference to FirmTech, a company that manufactures wearable sexual wellness devices and once counted GOP gubernatorial nominee Zach Lahn as an investor. Lahn maintains that the product was originally developed to monitor cardiovascular health and that he divested before the company shifted toward more sexually suggestive marketing. Sand has also pointed to Lahn's regular flights to Kansas, arguing that they betray tenuous ties to the state he's seeking to govern. Lahn, meanwhile, says that he lives full-time in Iowa, explaining that the flights are a product of him needing to shuttle children from a previous marriage between the two states. Lahn's campaign did not divulge where he attends church when asked by Fox News Digital. LGBTQ GROUP REVEALS WHICH DEM NOMINEE IS SPONSORING HALLOWEEN EVENT FEATURING DRAG SHOWS Plymouth’s progressive reputation is well-earned. In May 2025, Plymouth hosted drag queen "Flamy Grant" for a concert, according to advertisements for the event, bringing an artist whose broader catalog includes sexually explicit lyrics to the progressive Des Moines congregation. In one song, titled "Take a Chance on Me," not to be confused with the ABBA classic of the same name, Grant sings, "I’m a patient lover unless I finish first. And I expect you [to] finish me if the roles are reversed. I maintain the mystery of my sexual history." In another song, the drag queen complained about his childhood church, stating that "I guess the lesson there was God would only hear a prayer If it came from a person with a c---." The song continues to state that "secretly most men just fear the snatch" and praises Eve for disobeying God by eating the forbidden fruit. POWERFUL LGBTQ+ GROUP'S ENDORSEMENTS COULD TANK VULNERABLE DEMS OVER RADICAL YOUTH TRANS AGENDA About a year later, Plymouth promoted a drag event on its Facebook page at a nearby church billed as a "family-friendly karaoke fundraiser" headlined by drag queen "Tess Tura." Tura hosts a podcast where, among other topics, unprotected gay sex is discussed. In a similar vein, Plymouth invited transgender pastor Paula Stone Williams to serve as a guest pastor for one weekend in 2023, according to a local media report. At the time, Williams had recently published a book titled "As a Woman: What I learned about power, sex, and the patriarchy after I transitioned." VULNERABLE DEM'S CAMPAIGN PITCH CLASHES WITH 'RADICAL' VOTING RECORD ON TOP CULTURE WAR ISSUE Some of Plymouth’s pro-LGBTQ advocacy is directed at young children. Plymouth disclosed in a 2025 job posting that it partners with the Rainbow Faith Coalition, a group that says "LGBTQ+ identities are God-given, honored and celebrated," and that "[f]ully living into these identities in name, pronoun, relationship and gender expression is not a barrier to participation … in any areas of the faith community," including children’s programming and education. The church also offers Our Whole Lives programming, a sexuality education curriculum co-published by the Unitarian Universalist Association and the United Church of Christ, with classes beginning in first grade that address topics including sexuality, relationships, gender identity and sexual health. Similar to its theology, the church’s politics are decidedly liberal. TOP CONSERVATIVE GROUP UNVEILS FULL-COURT PRESS IN KEY BATTLEGROUND STATE TO EXPOSE ‘SHOCKING’ DEM PLATFORM In February 2025, for example, Plymouth’s pastors joined a protest in Iowa’s statehouse "to pray and stand up for our trans and gender nonconforming friends and neighbors," per a post on the church's Facebook page. A few years prior, church leadership participated in a pro-LGBTQ rally outside the statehouse, according to another church Facebook post. "Plymouth’s bold social justice presence is a hallmark in the community and is often cited as a reason for new members joining the congregation," a church job posting from 2025 reads. "We are committed to advancing justice, equity, and compassion in and beyond our community." Indeed, as the Supreme Court struck down Roe v. Wade, Plymouth mobilized to fight against pro-life legislation, supporting those fighting for "reproductive healthcare" and referring to women as "all who hold the potential to bear life." The church held a prayer vigil in support of abortion in May 2022 and rallied at the state capital in July 2023 to protest against efforts to regulate abortion. articles.title: Man hospitalized after being hit by ICE vehicle in west Houston, officials say

articles.body:
HOUSTON ( CW39 ) — A man was injured and taken to the hospital after being struck by a vehicle driven by Immigration and Customs Enforcement authorities in west Houston, the Harris County Sheriff’s Office said.

The incident happened around Saturday morning near Highway 6, the HCSO said.

Deputies said that ICE were in pursuit of a vehicle containing a wanted suspect. The pursuit was going southbound on Highway 6 when the suspected vehicle stopped and two men fled from the vehicle.

While trying to apprehend the passenger from the vehicle, ICE agents tried to box in the suspect near a building when one of the vehicles hit the suspect.

The 48-year-old man was taken to a local hospital, where his condition is unknown, but deputies believe the man suffered a broken leg. Deputies said that he is currently in ICE custody.

The HCSO said that their vehicular crimes unit is investigating the incident and will use surveillance video around the scene to determine what happened.

Harris County Precinct 4 Commissioner Lesley Briones issued a statement about the incident:

“I am horrified to learn that an ICE vehicle struck a man on Clay Road this morning in Precinct 4. While we wait to learn more, my prayers are with his family. Under the Trump administration, ICE has brought chaos and destruction to communities across our country. ICE must cooperate fully with the Harris County Sheriff’s Office and release all video evidence of this incident. We demand full transparency, accountability, and respect for the rule of law.”

articles.title: Vance’s sympathetic push exposes his 2028 ambitions
articles.summary: While Democrats continue surveying the field, their most likely Republican opponent has already begun staking out his lane to the White House.
articles.body:
Almost immediately after next month’s midterms, attention will turn to 2028, which figures to be an election without recent precedent. For the first time in more than a decade, Republicans will enter a presidential election without Donald Trump atop the ticket, forcing the party to define its identity and direction in a post-Trump era.

Democrats face a related challenge: They, too, lack a clear identity and future standard-bearer. Former Vice President Kamala Harris leads most national polls, yet donors and strategists are reportedly wary of another run after her 2024 performance.

That leaves a wide-open field, with roughly a dozen potential Democratic candidates trying to break through while the party remains caught between its progressive and establishment wings. But while Democrats continue surveying the field, their most likely Republican opponent has already begun staking out his lane to the White House.

Vice President JD Vance has assumed an increasingly public role in recent weeks, becoming, as Politico described , a “voice of patience and even empathy.” Vance has acknowledged voters’ deep frustration with the administration, particularly over the cost of living and the war with Iran. He has asked voters for patience, telling them “not to throw the baby out with the bathwater” if they disagree with the administration on individual policies.

That is a marked contrast with President Trump, who has dismissed affordability concerns as a “ hoax ,” given himself an A+ “on everything” and consistently paints a rosy picture of an economy that voters remain unhappy with.

At the same time, Vance has sought to deepen the Republicans’ populist turn while energizing his own political base. He has appealed to “America First” voters with attacks on “globalized liberalism,” “American elites” and the idea that free markets necessarily benefit Americans — an approach the New York Times called “New Right economics.”

On foreign policy — the issue on which Vance most clearly diverges from Trump — he has given voice to the Republicans’ increasingly isolationist, Israel-skeptical flank, including by leading the push for last summer’s ceasefire with Iran .

To be sure, the vice president’s unofficial role is to sell the administration’s agenda. But Trump has always been his own chief salesman. Vance is plainly attempting something more: making his own mark on the Republican Party ahead of 2028 and beyond.

Vice presidents often run as a continuation of the incumbent. Yet Trump is deeply unpopular, with just a 38 percent approval rating , and Vance is unlikely to replicate Trump’s charisma or personal bond with the Republican base, though that could change if he gets Trump’s endorsement.

Much as Harris has among Democrats, Vance has long led early 2028 polling on the Republican side, benefiting from his close association with Trump and support among MAGA voters. His average lead in 2028 nomination polls is roughly 16 points, according to RealClearPolitics . The base’s enthusiasm was evident at last month’s Republican midterm convention, where Vance drew thunderous applause and chants of “48” — a reference to his becoming the 48th president.

Unlike the Democrats’ field, however, the Republican field is currently quite narrow. Aside from Secretary of State Marco Rubio, virtually no other prospective candidate is viewed as a serious contender. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) and Donald Trump Jr. are the only other candidates who regularly top 5 percent in polls — Vance and Rubio are in a tier of their own.

Trump assembled an impressive coalition in 2024, particularly among Hispanic voters, but that support has eroded. Recent NBC polling put his approval among Hispanics at just 27 percent. It is difficult to see Vance improving substantially with these voters while he adheres to the party line on immigration and defends Immigration and Customs Enforcement overreach, including calling the ICE-involved shooting of Renee Good a “tragedy of her own making.”

Vance’s 2028 prospects are also inextricably linked to the Republican Party’s midterm performance — and Democrats currently lead the generic ballot by 8 points. New York Times-Siena polling in key Senate races in Texas, Alaska, New Hampshire, Ohio and Michigan also shows Democrats ahead, while even deep-red Iowa and Kansas are “neck and neck.”

Likewise, Emerson’s August survey suggested that independents are not yet sold on Vance. In hypothetical matchups against five leading Democrats, Rubio consistently outperformed the vice president. The contrast was especially notable against Harris and California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D). Vance trailed both, but Rubio led Harris by 5 points and was virtually tied with Newsom.

To Vance’s credit, his strategy is politically astute. As Trump’s natural heir, he likely sees an opportunity to steer Republicans toward his own brand of populism, while a more sympathetic posture could help him compete for independents.

He is also shrewdly aware that whoever Trump endorses will almost certainly win the party’s nomination, as Trump remains popular with Republicans in spite of his low poll numbers with the overall electorate.

Whether Vance succeeds remains to be seen. But by presenting a softer face of the administration while trying to steer the party in his preferred direction, he is revealing both his political instincts and the scale of his ambitions.

Douglas E. Schoen and Carly Cooperman are pollsters and partners with the public opinion company Schoen Cooperman Research based in New York. They are co-authors of the book “ America: Unite or Die . ”

articles.body:
Federal agents searched the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) on Monday morning as part of an ongoing criminal investigation .

Agents with Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) — the investigative arm of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) — carried out the search, a Justice Department spokesperson told NewsNation, The Hill’s sister network.

“This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation,” the Justice Department said in its statement.

The Hill has reached out to Omar’s office.

DOJ does not typically take major actions against candidates for office in the 60 days preceding an election. The midterm elections are in three weeks.

The search comes nearly a month after White House border czar Tom Homan confirmed a federal criminal investigation involving Omar.

“If someone committed an immigration violation, if someone committed marriage fraud or anything like that, regardless if they’re a congressman or not, no one’s above the law. So, I’ll leave it at that. We’ll let HSI, Homeland Security Investigations, continue the investigation,” Homan said during an appearance on Fox News.

HSI is an elite investigative unit with ICE that has traditionally been focused on combatting crime networks involved in human and weapons trafficking as well as other major crimes across borders, such as antiquities smuggling and cyber and financial crimes.

Republicans have lobbed allegations of widespread immigration fraud within Minnesota’s Somali community.

Several GOP voices have also relayed skepticism about one of Omar’s past marriages.

That includes Vice President Vance, who in May said, “You read the things about Ilhan Omar … who she married and whether she didn’t marry this person or that person. It certainly seems like something fishy is there, but everybody’s entitled to equal justice under the law.”

Omar in the past has denied allegations — now roughly 10 years old that first circulated in right-wing media — that she married her brother.

The Justice Department has boosted its components focused on immigration fraud and also started a denaturalization campaign to rescind American citizenship from anyone who misrepresents details in applying for citizenship.

A member of the progressive crew “The Squad,” Omar came to the U.S. as a child with her family from Somalia as they sought asylum amid the civil war that spurred widespread displacement. She received citizenship in 2000.

President Trump and other prominent allies have levied numerous allegations against the congresswoman over her immigration status, accusing the Somali native of fraudulently obtaining U.S. citizenship, which she has denied, and openly seeking to have her removed from the country.

The administration announced it was investigating Omar last year for alleged immigration fraud after Trump and others claimed without evidence that Omar married her brother in order to obtain U.S. citizenship.

The progressive lawmaker has repeatedly clashed with Trump over his administration’s policies, and tensions heightened further after the president attacked Somali people in connection to Minnesota’s fraud scandal, accusing refugees from the African nation of “completely taking over the once great state of Minnesota.”

The president also lashed out at Omar in a Cabinet meeting, calling her “garbage” while saying he did not want Somali people in the U.S., and at one point he said Somalia “stinks.”

“We could go one way or the other, and we’re going to go the wrong way if we keep taking in garbage into our country,” Trump said. “Ilhan Omar is garbage. She’s garbage. Her friends are garbage. These aren’t people who work. These aren’t people who say, ‘Let’s go, come on, let’s make this place great.’”

“His obsession with me is creepy. I hope he gets the help he desperately needs,” Omar said in response to Trump’s attacks, which were also condemned by officials in Minnesota.

articles.title: Gavin Newsom can commute all California death sentences and still become president
articles.summary: Such an act would be the single most significant anti-death penalty act in all of American history. Never before has a political leader had the chance to save as many lives of people awaiting execution.
articles.body:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom has a chance to make history by commuting all death sentences in his state. He can and should do so by sparing the lives of the 563 California prisoners on death row .

Such an act would be the single most significant anti-death penalty act in all of American history. Never before has a political leader had the chance to save as many lives of people awaiting execution.

Coming at a moment when the nation’s attention is fixed on the cruelty of capital punishment , a mass commutation of the nation’s largest death row population would be a lightning bolt. It would be wind in the sails of abolitionists and provide political cover for governors in other death penalty states to empty their death rows.

And Newsom can solidify his already substantial standing as a leading voice against capital punishment without damaging his political prospects should he decide to run for president.

To get a sense of the magnitude and significance of a mass commutation in California, consider the following. Over the last two decades, 11 states have abolished the death penalty : Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Illinois, Maryland, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Virginia and Washington. In all of those states combined, the total death row population at the time of abolition was 69.

Or consider that to this point in American history, the largest mass clemency for people sentenced to death occurred as a result of the Supreme Court’s 1972 decision in Furman v. Georgia, which invalidated the death sentences of 629 people who had been sentenced under constitutionally defective laws.

In 2003, Illinois Gov. George Ryan (R) emptied his state’s death row by granting clemency to 167 people. And just before leaving office, President Biden commuted 37 death sentences to life in prison without parole.

While California currently has a moratorium on executions and has not executed a prisoner in 20 years, if Newsom issues a universal clemency in California, that single gesture would reduce the number of people on death row in the entire country by one-fourth.

In the Golden State, the path for such a clemency is complicated. As The New York Times explains, “Under California law, a governor can unilaterally grant clemency to a prisoner with a single conviction, but the State Supreme Court must approve a clemency request for inmates with multiple felony convictions.” However, whatever that court might do, Newsom could still spare the lives of more people than any other governor or president ever has.

The governor has been a persistent and outspoken critic of capital punishment . Newsom says that “The intentional killing of another person is wrong and … our death penalty system has been, by all measures, a failure.” But news reports suggest that Newsom is weighing the impact a universal clemency might have on his campaign if he decides to run for president.

The evidence suggests it would not significantly damage his political prospects.

During the 2020 presidential nominating campaign, almost every candidate for the Democratic presidential nomination opposed the death penalty , and in the run-up to the election that fall, Joe Biden was open about his opposition to capital punishment.

Today, while a slim majority of the American public supports the death penalty, most Americans recognize the serious flaws in the death penalty system.

And if the result of the 2028 campaign were to depend on the results in so-called swing states, many of them would seem to be fertile ground for a candidate with a record of opposition to the death penalty. Two of those seven states (Michigan and Wisconsin) abolished capital punishment a long time ago.

Like California, Pennsylvania has a moratorium on executions currently in place and hasn’t executed anyone since 1999. Its governor, Josh Shapiro (D), opposes the death penalty and has called on the legislature to abolish it . He remains one of the most popular governors in the country.

The death penalty in North Carolina is on hold because of pending court challenges and has not executed anyone in two decades. Though he is not an abolitionist, former governor and current candidate for the U.S. Senate, Roy Cooper (D), commuted the death sentences of 15 people.

Like North Carolina, Nevada has the death penalty on the books but hasn’t executed anyone since 2006 .

That leaves two of the swing states, Arizona and Georgia, where the death penalty is still legal and where executions have been carried out recently.

But in Georgia, U.S. Sen. Raphael Warnock (D) has been an outspoken opponent of capital punishment, calling it “The final failsafe of white supremacy.” He still managed to win his seat in Congress.

Finally, in Arizona, public support for the death penalty has declined in recent years, as have the number of new death sentences being imposed in the state .

All of this suggests that Newsom has room to maneuver as he considers whether to follow his conscience and use his clemency power to deliver a devastating blow to America’s death penalty system. Should he do so, he will vindicate the hopes that the late Pope Francis expressed when Newsom visited him in 2024.

As The New York Times notes , when he saw Newsom, the Pope “flashed a thumbs up” and dubbed the governor his “’death penalty man.’”

Austin Sarat is the William Nelson Cromwell Professor of Jurisprudence and Political Science at Amherst College .

articles.title: Trump says 'days of plunder are over' in renewed push for Columbus Day
articles.summary: President Trump has for years pushed back on criticism of Christopher Columbus. Here's what he said recently.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump declared an end to the "plunder" of statues of explorer Christopher Columbus in renewed comments opposing criticism of the historical figure.

In an Oct. 11 Truth Social post celebrating Columbus Day , which is on Oct. 12 this year, Trump said Italian Americans were "forced to suffer" as statues of Columbus were removed across the country in recent years. Critics of the explorer have argued that honoring him glorifies the exploitation and genocide of native peoples.

"Radical Left Dumocrats, Socialists, and Communists rampaged through our cities and towns ripping down almost all of the beautiful statues of Christopher Columbus. Well, those days of plunder are over, and the statues are back, more magnificent than ever," Trump wrote.

Some cities and states have shifted to celebrating the second Monday in October as Indigenous Peoples' Day instead of Columbus Day, the federal holiday that has honored the explorer for more than a century.

While former President Joe Biden issued the first presidential proclamation for Indigenous Peoples' Day in 2021, Trump has pushed to refocus the day toward Columbus since returning to office.

Here's what Trump has said about Columbus Day and why the day is controversial.

Trump says he 'resurrected' Christopher Columbus

Trump's latest post came days after he commemorated Columbus Day at an Oct. 9 event . There, the president attributed his support from Italian Americans to his backing of the Italian explorer.

"The reason I get all of the Italian vote, I really believe – I didn't do it for this reason – I resurrected Christopher Columbus," he said.

The president cited a new statue of Columbus that went up on White House grounds earlier this year. After protesters toppled a sculpture of Columbus in Baltimore in 2020, officials installed a 13-foot replica of the piece, made from fragments of the original sculpture, in March in front of the Eisenhower Executive Office Building.

"In this administration, we know that Christopher Columbus is – to us he's a hero," Trump said.

He also called for the return of a Columbus statue that was removed from outside city hall in Columbus, Ohio, in 2020.

Trump's push for Columbus Day is not new

Trump has for years argued that Columbus' legacy is mistreated.

"Sadly, in recent years, radical activists have sought to undermine Christopher Columbus's legacy," he said in a 2020 Columbus Day proclamation. "These extremists seek to replace discussion of his vast contributions with talk of failings, his discoveries with atrocities, and his achievements with transgressions."

In April 2025 , a few months into his second term, Trump declared that he was "bringing Columbus Day back from the ashes" in a Truth Social post.

In another proclamation signed in October 2025 , Trump wrote that Columbus "has been a prime target of a vicious and merciless campaign to erase our history, slander our heroes, and attack our heritage."

Columbus Day is still marked as a federal holiday , but some states and cities instead honor the day as Indigenous Peoples' Day .

The push recognizes that Native Americans populated the country before Columbus' arrival. It also acknowledges the atrocities – including devastating loss of life, tradition and lands – that resulted from European contact in the Americas, according to the Smithsonian National Museum of the American Indian .

In 2021, Biden became the first president to issue a proclamation recognizing Indigenous Peoples' Day.

"For generations, Federal policies systematically sought to assimilate and displace Native people and eradicate Native cultures. Today, we recognize Indigenous peoples' resilience and strength as well as the immeasurable positive impact that they have made on every aspect of American society," Biden wrote in the proclamation.

Contributing: Zac Anderson, Michelle Del Rey

Melina Khan is a national trending reporter for USA TODAY. Keep up with her on X @melinakh and Instagram @bymelinakhan .

articles.title: Trump’s racial politics shape midterm elections
articles.summary: As the Florida midterm elections approach, analysts suggest that shifting racial dynamics and reactions to President Trump’s immigration policies may play a decisive role in the outcome.
articles.body:
“Oh Juan, why do you have to make everything about race?” That is a common complaint I get on social media. But how can anyone honestly discuss the Florida midterm elections without talking about race?

Let’s start with Latino voters, before looking at Black and white voters. President Trump’s national approval among Latino voters is way underwater at 27 percent, according to NBC . That is a political shock, given that Trump won the Latino vote in Florida in 2024 as well as the majority of Latino men nationwide.

In the last two years, Trump’s numbers with Latinos, about 20 percent of the state’s voters, have fallen off the map. His polling with Latinos is now so bad that Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar (R-Fla.) ran an advertisement separating herself from Trump’s immigration enforcement.

“Mr. President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far,” Salazar said in the ad . “The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today.”

Republicans like Salazar are desperate to protect their political lives.

Who can forget that last year the Cuban-born leader of “Latinos for Trump” himself faced deportation by ICE? The co-founder of “Latinas for Trump,” sounded a similar note last year. She wrote : “This is not what we voted for. … What we are witnessing are arbitrary measures to hunt down people who are complying with their immigration hearings.”

Florida cities and even rural farms have been the scene of ICE tearing at the Latino population by wrongfully arresting and deporting people without criminal records.

Sixty-six percent of Latinos in a recent NBC poll agree that Trump’s handling of illegal immigration has “gone too far.”

Florida’s Republican governor and legislature did nothing to protest Trump’s policies and even endorsed some of them . So did the state’s Republican congressional delegation, including a Black man now running for governor and a white woman now running for the U.S. Senate.

U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fla.), the gubernatorial candidate, stood by the immigration raids executed by Trump’s immigration officers. It fit his efforts to prove that despite being Black, he is loyal to Trump and his hard-right, MAGA-brand conservatism.

Donalds had no signature legislative accomplishments in five years in Congress. But he was one of only two Black representatives to vote against impeaching Trump for inciting an attempt to overturn the results of the 2020 election. The Trump supporters who violently surged into the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6 included a man waving a large Confederate Flag .

Also silent on Trump’s aggressive immigration actions is the white woman running for Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s former Senate seat.

Sen. Ashley Moody (R-Fla.), formerly Florida’s attorney general, is best known for always standing with Trump. She signed on to a lawsuit contesting Trump’s defeat in the 2020 election . To this day, she refuses to concede that Trump lost.

Moody’s opponent is a Black woman, state Rep. Angie Nixon (D), a member of the Democratic Socialists of America and a strong critic of Trump’s immigration policy, willing to point out the masked ICE agents grabbing Latinos off the street, often only on the basis of their accents and skin color. Nixon is also speaking out against ICE deportations of Haitians, noting Florida is home to the largest Haitian community of any state.

“They fled horrific violence and political instability to build lives here,” she said recently .”

She favors impeaching Trump and his Cabinet officers because “they’ve all committed impeachable offenses,” Nixon told The Bulwark . Unlike Moody or Donalds, she is willing to address the fact that Trump smeared Mexicans as “rapists.”

Nixon can also talk to Latinos in the state about how Trump has left Cuba stalled without adequate oil or food. Unlike her opponents, she does not ignore or excuse that Trump famously shared Thanksgiving dinner at his Florida estate with the white supremacist podcaster Nick Fuentes.

Donalds’ opponent in the governor’s race is a white man and former Republican, David Jolly. Unlike Donalds, he is clear in standing opposed to Trump’s use of race to stir populist anger among his MAGA supporters.

Jolly was one of the first Republicans to separate himself from Trump in 2015 when Trump proposed to ban all Muslims from entering the U.S.

According to the last Census , Florida is about 50 percent non-Hispanic white, 30 percent Hispanic and 15 percent Black.

Its large Hispanic population makes it a key measure inside polls showing a potential wave of victories for Democrats in the midterms.

A prime example outside of Florida is in the Republican stronghold of Texas, where Latino voters have a Latina running a tight race against the incumbent governor.

Inside Florida, a strong showing of Latinos voting for Democrats could lift Democratic House candidates across the state’s 28 congressional districts. The seats most likely to flip are in South Florida, which has the largest concentration of Hispanic voters.

National Democrats had better start paying attention and investing resources . If they turn Florida, it will open new paths to the presidency in 2028, lined with changing racial attitudes.

Keep in mind that Florida voted twice for President Barack Obama.

My social media critics are right: not everything is about race. But this year’s midterms in Florida are absolutely about fallout from Trump’s racial politics.

Juan Williams is senior political analyst for Fox News Channel and a prize-winning civil rights historian. He is the author of the new book “ New Prize for These Eyes: The Rise of America’s Second Civil Rights Movement . “

articles.title: Immigration officials search Congresswoman Ilhan Omar home
articles.summary: Omar was first elected to Congress in 2018, and is an outspoken critic of President Donald Trump.
articles.body:
US immigration agents searched the home of Minnesota Representative Ilhan Omar on Monday morning as part of a "criminal investigation".

Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents "executed a judicially authorized search warrant" for the home in the Washington, DC, area, a US justice department spokesperson told the BBC.

The search "is part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation," the spokesperson said but no further details were given.

Omar was born in Somalia and came to the US aged eight fleeing war. First elected to Congress in 2018, she is running for reelection next month, and is an outspoken critic of President Donald Trump.

The US Congress is currently out of session and it is unclear if Omar was at the home. The BBC has contacted Omar for comment.

While the nature of the criminal investigation remains unclear, it is not the first time her immigration records have been scrutinised by Republicans. Earlier this year, fellow Congresswoman Nancy Mace of South Carolina unsuccessfully filed a subpoena of her records.

Last month, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told a conservative podcaster "something is going to happen", alleging that Omar had previously married her brother "to try to bring him to the United States." Her brother now lives in London, he said.

Separately, the White House border tsar Tom Homan told Fox News Omar was being investigated for unspecified immigration violations.

Omar, a Democrat, denied these allegations last month. "I will say it again so it's as clear as possible: I'm not at all worried about these investigations, because they are complete shams," she said in a campaign fundraising email.

She has been the target of Trump's insults and the president previously suggested that she "should go back" to Somalia and at times said she should be deported. US citizenship is required to serve as a US House Representative.

Omar has responded to Trump's insults and attacks describing them as "unhealthy and creepy obsession."

The president has also spoken unfavourably about the Somali American community. Last week, he wrote on social media that Minnesota "is being taken over by Somali immigrants" and said "the people of Minnesota must fight back."

Omar is the first Somali-American elected to the US House of Representatives and she represents a district in the Minneapolis area. She and Michigan Representative Rashida Tlaib were the first Muslim women elected to Congress.

She won the 2024 election with 74% of the vote. The timing of Monday's raid — 22 days to the November midterm elections which will decide the balance of power for the next two years — is likely to raise concerns from Democrats.

The justice department has a longstanding policy of refraining from most enforcement action that is "likely to raise an issue or the perception" that it was being brought for the purpose of affecting any election or disadvantage a candidate.

articles.title: Rep. Ilhan Omar’s home searched by federal agents in criminal probe
articles.summary: Federal agents searched Rep. Ilhan Omar’s home in Washington, D.C., on Monday morning, according to two people familiar with the investigation.
articles.body: Federal agents searched Rep. Ilhan Omar’s home in Washington, D.C., on Monday morning, according to two people familiar with the investigation. Homeland Security Investigations, part of the Department of Homeland Security that conducts criminal probes, “executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the Department of Justice,” a DOJ spokesperson said in a statement. “This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation.” The statement did not specify that the warrant was related to Omar and did not provide further information about the nature of the investigation. A person familiar with the investigation said the probe is part of a years-long criminal investigation that involves whistleblowers. A Homeland Security Investigations team of about 15 to 20 agents were seen leaving the house late in the morning. A spokesperson for Omar, D-Minn., did not immediately respond to NBC News’ request for comment on the search, which was first reported by Fox News. The White House and Department of Homeland Security referred questions about the search to the Justice Department. The timing puts the search under added scrutiny: There are 22 days until the midterm elections. Omar is running for re-election in Minnesota. There’s longstanding Justice Department practice that tells prosecutors to be especially careful about actions near an election that could appear to help or hurt a candidate. There is no blanket rule barring the department from acting within 60 days before an election, but that’s long been an unwritten practice. The written policy says prosecutors and agents cannot time investigative steps or public statements to influence an election and directs them to seek guidance when the timing could raise questions. In 2016, then-FBI Director James Comey publicly disclosed developments in the email probe of Democratic presidential nominee Hillary Clinton just 11 days before the presidential election. After he took office, Trump fired Comey, and the administration justified his dismissal by saying he had violated longstanding principles of the Justice Department by announcing his conclusions about the Clinton case. Trump said he would have fired Comey “regardless” of the Justice Department memo outlining what it said were his missteps. Late last month, the Justice Department’s Office of the Inspector General recommended that the department’s leaders should prioritize giving guidance to agents and prosecutors on actions that could “foreseeably affect an impending election.” Those include “the taking of overt investigative steps, indictments, public announcements, or other actions” that could have such an impact, according to the recommendation, which was initially part of a 2018 report on the DOJ and FBI’s actions leading up to the 2016 election. Omar is running for re-election, and the midterms are less than a month away. Last month, border czar Tom Homan told Fox News that Omar was being investigated by the Department of Homeland Security. “If someone committed immigration violation, if someone committed marriage fraud or anything like that, regardless if they’re a congressman or not, no one’s above the law,” Homan said at the time. “So, I’ll leave it at that. We’ll let HSI, Homeland Security Investigations, continue the investigation.” Omar immigrated to the U.S. from Somalia as a child. She fled Somalia’s civil war with her family when she was eight years old and stayed in a Kenyan refugee camp for four years before moving to the U.S., her website details. President Donald Trump has frequently lashed out at Omar, who is a member of a progressive faction of women in Congress collectively known as the “squad,” criticizing her over her liberal positions. Trump targeted both Omar and Somalians over the weekend during his remarks at a rally in Tennessee. “How about Ilhan Omar? She comes from Somalia,” he said Saturday as the crowd booed. The president went to characterize the country as ungoverned and lawless, saying “all they have is crime and squalor.” “What they’ve done to Minnesota, these people from Somalia, what they’ve done to Minnesota should never be allowed,” he added. “And let’s see what happens. JD Vance and our people are looking at it very strongly.” Early this year, Trump said that the Justice Department and Congress are “looking at” the congresswoman. The president has also repeatedly targeted Minnesota over fraud scandals that roiled the state. Last week, Trump told Minnesotans to “fight back” against immigrants from Somalia. He claimed in a Truth Social post that the state “is being taken over by Somali Immigrants.” One of the most high-profile fraud cases was a $250 million case where perpetrators allegedly stole money from a Covid-related program that provided food for children. Since then, the Justice Department announced criminal charges against more than a dozen people in Minnesota over alleged social services fraud. The former leader of Feeding Our Future, the non-profit at the center of the $250 million fraud case, is white. Most of the defendants in the related cases are of Somali descent, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office, a fact Trump has highlighted as he has repeatedly disparaged people of Somali descent. Omar blamed Trump’s rhetoric against her and Somali immigrants as a contributing factor in an attack on her at a town hall event in January.

articles.title: Plan B for Trump’s election intimidation: An iron fist in a velvet glove
articles.summary: While Gen. Dan Caine testified that the U.S. military has no plans to be at polling places, experts warn that military leaders will need to utilize specific rules for the use of force to mitigate potential voter intimidation if the Insurrection Act is invoked.
articles.body:
Gen. Dan Caine, the nation’s senior-most military leader, recently told Sen Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) that the U.S. military has “no plans” to be at polling places in November. But President Trump has made it impossible to dismiss fears of military interference.

To the contrary, his persistent assault on the integrity of the voting process, his suggestion that Republicans “should take over the voting in at least 15 places,” and his refusal to rule out invoking the Insurrection Act have led many to begin bracing for an imminent collision.

Americans across the country are worrying that their constitutionally-assured right to vote will be curtailed by Trump’s increasingly frantic search for anything that will preserve his party’s congressional majorities.

The bar for legally deploying troops to polling places is high. Under the Posse Comitatus Act, the president cannot use federal military troops for law enforcement purposes. Meanwhile, federal law makes it a crime to post “troops or armed men” at polling site, but exceptions exist. The Insurrection Act permits the president to deploy troops in response to “unlawful obstructions, combinations, or assemblages” or “domestic violence, unlawful combination, or conspiracy.” Troops or armed men can be legally deployed at polling sites to “repel enemies of the United States.”

If the president wants to deploy troops to election sites, he can easily come up with a set of fake facts that satisfies both legal loopholes.

Most senior commanders understand the damage that can be done if troops are deployed to polling places; not only would it present real threats to democracy but it could subject them — not the president — to criminal prosecution.

In his testimony before Congress, the commander responsible for the domestic use of military forces acknowledged that laws prohibit deploying troops to polling sites and asserted that he would refuse orders that violate them.

However, if resistance fails and the president and his Office of Legal Counsel concoct legal and factual justifications for deploying troops to polling sites, military commanders and their judge advocates can mitigate the impacts of these actions by exercising good judgment.

First, state and local officials and commanders must be transparent with each other and with the media about what is happening at every polling site. Commanders will need to display moral courage if the facts they perceive on the ground are different from those Trump and his minions are peddling. If ordered to polling places, they must first and foremost focus on de-escalation.

They must also resist the inevitable pressure of mission creep. Exceptions to federal law allowing deployment of troops to polling places are very narrow. Commanders cannot let their responses exceed those narrow limits. For example, federal troops deployed to quell discontent cannot seize voting equipment, ballots, or otherwise interfere in election processes.

If the secretary of Defense orders commanders to wield an iron fist, they can and must refuse to intimidate anyone or to interfere in the voting process, donning velvet gloves instead. “ Rules for use of force ” — which are rules that are established by commanders that troops must follow when deployed domestically — must stipulate that servicemembers must be neither seen nor heard by voters unless there is an actual civil disturbance that exceeds law enforcement agencies’ ability to respond. These rules must also acknowledge the limits of the legal authorities upon which the deployment is based.

For example, they must stipulate that troops may only be used to address physical disturbances at the polls. They must agree that troops may not do anything that might intimidate voters, including detaining them for any reason other than to quell disturbances. (For example, they may not look for or detain suspected non-citizens, enforce voting procedures or observe voting processes.)

The public should be concerned that Trump may deploy the military as part of his effort to “take over” voting in many locations. But that concern need not translate to fear that troops will adversely impact the election. If existing legal guardrails fail, there is still a Plan B. The military officers ordered to command those troops and the judge advocates advising them can mitigate whatever intimidation Trump seeks to achieve.

Steven Lepper is a retired U.S. Air Force major general, Dan Maurer is a retired U.S. Army lieutenant colonel and Eugene R. Fidell is a military law expert.

articles.title: Democrats see new chances to flip red states — but a $400M GOP spending advantage could derail their plans
articles.summary: Republicans outspend Democrats by $400 million ahead of Election Day, forcing Senate Majority PAC to make tough choices across nine battlegrounds.
articles.body: With just over three weeks to go until Election Day, more and more red states and congressional districts appear in reach for the Democrats, as they work to win back House and Senate majorities from the Republicans in the midterms. But a massive Republican spending advantage threatens to complicate those ambitions. Republican campaigns, committees and aligned groups have outspent their Democratic counterparts by $400 million so far this election cycle, according to AdImpact, a leading political advertising tracking firm. The disparity is forcing Democrats to make difficult decisions about where to invest and how much to spend as the party tries to expand the electoral map. "We are being outspent by the Republicans. That's just a fact," Lauren French, communications director at the Senate Majority PAC, told Fox News Digital. "In many of these states, they have really transactionalized elections, so they have monopoly money to play with, whereas we are working with real resources." DEMOCRATS THINK A BLUE WAVE IS FORMER - HERE ARE THREE FACTORS THAT COULD STOP IT The latest Fox News Power Rankings shifted GOP-dominated South Carolina from Solid to Likely Republican. The Senate showdown in reliably Republican Kansas is Lean Republican, while the races in red-leaning Alaska, Iowa, Ohio and Texas are rated toss-ups. "Senate Majority PAC has resources to compete, and we are very happy that we're able to be in 9 battleground states," French said. The super PAC is the leading outside group supporting Democratic Senate candidates and incumbents and is aligned with longtime Democratic leader Sen. Chuck Schumer. French highlighted record-setting fundraising over the past three months, but added, "of course, more recess resources would be helpful." With the latest polls from Fox News and other organizations showing Democrats increasingly competitive across the Senate map, the party is pleading for more money. "Last month a pro-Trump PAC reserved $10 million in New Hampshire advertising, and we’re being outspent 3-to-1," reads a fundraising pitch to supporters by Rep. Chris Pappas, the Democratic Senate nominee in swing state New Hampshire. WHO'S UP AND WHO'S DOWN IN THE LATEST FOX NEWS MIDTERM POWER RANKINGS Senate Majority PAC is rushing some of its record fundraising into the newly competitive battlegrounds. And American Bridge PAC, a Democrat-aligned group, recently pumped over $20 million into South Carolina and Kansas, as well as competitive races in two other red states, Florida and Mississippi. But the Democratic groups are being outspent by their Republican-aligned counterparts, thanks to major expenditures by Senate Leadership Fund, the President Donald Trump-allied MAGA Inc. and a super PAC bankrolled by Elon Musk. "The hard reality is there isn't enough funding to protect the toss-up states and also heavily invest in the red-leaning states where we're playing offense," a veteran Democratic Senate operative who requested anonymity to speak candidly told Fox News Digital." French told Fox News Digital "This is the time in the campaign season where everyone really has to make some of those belt-tightening decisions, and that's why we're looking at every race really closely to make sure we have enough resources to get to the majority, but we're also not leaving anyone shortchanged." House Democrats are facing a similar predicament. A memo from the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee (DCCC) shared with donors warned that Republicans "are now flooding districts across our battlefield with MAGA Inc. and Trump super PAC money that we simply cannot match." DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB The memo, which was obtained by Fox News Digital, requested an additional $17 million that was needed by Oct. 22 "to close the sale" in what they described as "winnable races." The GOP is fighting political history, which has traditionally seen the party in power in Washington lose congressional seats during midterm election years. Add to that a challenging political climate fueled by persistent inflation Americans see at the grocery store, high gas prices tied to what polls show is an unpopular war with Iran and Trump's negative approval ratings. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER But the Republicans' financial advantage has allowed GOP campaigns and allied groups to spend more on political advertising nationally. "Thanks to the tireless efforts of Leader John Thune, Senate Leadership Fund has amassed a financial advantage that neither party has had before. SLF will continue to invest unprecedented resources across the map to maintain the Republican Senate majority," Senate Leadership Fund communications director Chris Gustafson told Fox News Digital. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Veteran GOP strategist Jesse Hunt told Fox News Digital that "Republican outside groups will have played a decisive role in positive Republican performance if they have a good election night despite what is strong headwinds working against them." "This is not an advantage Republicans typically have and it's definitely a contributing factor to a lot of candidates on the ballot right now keeping their races close," Hunt emphasized.

articles.title: Johnson planning to remain GOP leader in ‘unlikely scenario’ Republicans lose House
articles.summary: Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) said he plans to remain as the leader of the Republican conference in the “unlikely scenario” that the GOP loses control of the House. “I want to be of my highest and best use to God in my country, and I feel like at this stage of life, I’m doing what…
articles.body:
Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) said he plans to remain as the leader of the Republican conference in the “unlikely scenario” that the GOP loses control of the House.

“I want to be of my highest and best use to God in my country, and I feel like at this stage of life, I’m doing what I’m called to do, and so I intend to lead as Speaker,” Johnson told CBS News’s Robert Costa in an exclusive interview. “Heaven forbid, I don’t think it’s going to happen, so I don’t spend any time thinking about it.”

He added, “But in the unlikely scenario where we lost the majority, I would expect my colleagues would ask me to continue leading this conference, even if we have divided government.”

Johnson’s remarks come just a few days after he floated the possibility of returning to Louisiana if Republicans lose the midterms in an interview with Fox News.

“It’s just hilarious,” the Speaker told CBS, when asked about the speculation that his remark quickly sparked.

“What I was trying to say to them is that throughout my whole life, my number one objective is to be of my highest and best use to God and to my country, and that’s always what I’ve thought,” the Louisiana Republican continued. “And I was trying to make the point that if God has a different design, then we’ll follow that. But what I believe is, I’m going to be the Speaker of the House for at least two more years.”

Asked about the fact that some Speakers left Congress after their party lost control, he told CBS, “I’m going to continue to serve my highest best use to God in country, and I believe right now, as we’re sitting here, that’s the Speaker of the House.”

“And if we lost the majority, I don’t think that that position that I have would change. I think I would stay right there,” Johnson added.

Some GOP lawmakers and aides previously told The Hill that there could be a potential push to support someone other than Johnson as leader if the party suffers major losses in the midterms.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) said last week that Johnson will “ultimately have to make a decision about what comes next.”

“I can say that the American people are about to retire Mike Johnson and the Republican majority in the House and possibly even in the Senate,” Jeffries said.

Decision Desk HQ, a partner of The Hill, currently gives Democrats a 76 percent chance of winning control of the lower chamber of Congress.

articles.title: Alito’s denial of judicial bias is a joke on the American people
articles.summary: The right-wing Supreme Court majority — Alito and Clarence Thomas hold down its right-most edge — was built explicitly to further a political agenda.
articles.body:
I don’t think of Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito as a particularly funny guy. But his recent interview with CBS News legal correspondent Jan Crawford made me laugh out loud.

“We are not part of any political movement, and we are not attempting to further any political agenda,” Alito said.

Alito’s claim is hilarious in an absurdist deadpan sort of way. But the laughter it provokes is not happy laughter. It’s the kind of grunt that pops out of your mouth when you hear President Trump spout some ridiculous thing. It’s preposterous that he is our president, and yet there he is.

When it comes to Alito’s claim, the history is clear. The right-wing Supreme Court majority — Alito and Clarence Thomas hold down its right-most edge — was built explicitly to further a political agenda.

The Federalist Society, the Heritage Foundation and the whole massive right-wing infrastructure built over the past 50 years is the fruit of a long-term campaign by corporations, foundations and wealthy individuals to amass enough political and legal power to reverse a century of progressive advances .

Movement leaders set out to overturn decades of precedent and return the country to a pre-New Deal, pre- Civil Rights Act version of reality. A reality in which the federal government doesn’t have much power to interfere with corporations doing whatever they want to workers or the environment, the bargaining and political power of worker unions has been brutally undermined and the rights of historically marginalized communities are ignored.

When Trump was elected for the first time, right-wing activists were giddy that his judicial nominees would give them the power to “ fundamentally change America .”

And that was on top of what court conservatives, including Alito, had already done to democracy in decisions like Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission, which made it virtually impossible to protect our elections from people and corporations with unlimited wealth, and Shelby County v. Holder , which started the court’s gutting of the Voting Rights Act .

When President Barack Obama criticized the Citizens United decision during his 2010 State of the Union speech , warning that it would open the floodgates for special interests, including foreign corporations, “to spend without limit in our elections,” Alito shook his head and mouthed , “Not true.” History has proven that Obama was right. and the impact of Citizens United and other rulings impairing efforts to regulate money flowing into elections has been enormous.

Speaking of political agendas, Alito wrote the 2022 decision overturning Roe v. Wade . He has also been central to the dismantling of the Voting Rights Act , a gift to Republican politicians eager to increase their power by gerrymandering away political representation for Black and brown voters. Earlier this year, Alito authored the opinion in Louisiana v. Callais , which the dissenting justices noted had made a key provision of the Voting Rights Act “ all but a dead letter .”

Alito has been a long-time advocate for the “unitary executive” — a right-wing theory for virtually unchecked presidential power. This Supreme Court majority has made it our reality , allowing Trump to turn independent agencies into instruments of his personal and political vendettas.

Alito has spoken frequently at events for the Federalist Society and other right-wing groups, brushing aside ethical concerns about “ judicial influence buying ” raised by public interest organizations.

There is really no question that right-wing politicians and activists view the federal courts as an instrument of their political agenda.

Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) became a hero to the hard right when, as Senate majority leader, he refused to allow the Senate to even consider President Barack Obama’s nomination to fill the Supreme Court vacancy created by the death of Antonin Scalia.

After Trump’s first election, McConnell and other right-wing operatives openly gloated about how many judicial vacancies Trump would be able to fill because McConnell and Senate Republicans obstructed and slow-walked judicial nominees during the last two years of Obama’s presidency. Republican senators have done the opposite for Trump, rushing to approve even his least qualified and most nakedly partisan nominees for lifetime federal judgeships.

Trump has complained harshly when the court — but not Alito — has resisted a few of his most blatantly unconstitutional moves. Trump has only praise for Alito, who has been a reliable vote and a rhetorical mouthpiece for the administration’s positions.

Alito can say it’s “ offensive ” to suggest that he’s the MAGA movement’s man on the court. But it would be a joke to pretend otherwise.

That’s one of many good reasons voters should give Democrats a Senate majority in these midterm elections. If Republicans maintain their control of the Senate, President Trump will continue to fill the courts with judges who make Americans’ lives less affordable and more subject to the authoritarian impulses of the president and his corporate and big tech backers.

And he’ll be sure to fill any Supreme Court vacancies with people like Alito, who he can count on to let him get away with anything.

Svante Myrick is president of People For the American Way .

articles.body:
Most Americans regardless of party oppose betting on election results through prediction markets such as Kalshi or Polymarket, according to a new survey.

A Reuters/Ipsos poll , released Monday, found that 60 percent of respondents did not support betting on election results, as the midterm elections near. Another 13 percent said they support betting, while 24 percent were unsure and 3 percent skipped the question.

Prediction markets allow people to place wagers on the outcome of various events, from elections to sports to the economy.

Among Republican respondents, 61 percent opposed election-result betting, 16 percent were supportive, 23 percent were unsure and 1 percent skipped the question. Just less than 70 percent of Democratic respondents were against betting on elections, while 12 percent approved, 18 percent were unsure and 1 percent skipped the question, the survey found.

The results differ when considering betting in other markets. Roughly 43 percent of respondents opposed betting on professional sports , 29 percent approve it, 25 percent were unsure and 4 percent did not answer.

Broken down by party, about 44 percent of Republican respondents and 50 percent of Democrats opposed betting on sports. Another 33 percent of GOP and 29 percent of Democratic respondents supported this kind of wagering.

Prediction markets jumped in popularity around the 2024 presidential elections, in which $3.7 billion was spent on Polymarket’s “ Presidential Election Winner 2024 ,” according to the platform. Around $1.3 billion was wagered on President Trump winning the election on Polymarket alone, while $1.03 billion was spent on betting former Vice President Kamala Harris would win the election, the data shows.

A Polymarket spokesperson told The Hill, “Most Americans are deeply disenchanted with our information ecosystem, because it’s often impossible to find the truth and avoid being scammed.”

“Prediction markets are a way to get unbiased, accurate information about the events that impact our lives,” the spokesperson continued. “Recognition of the public value of prediction markets is growing, but they’re still brand new to most, and it’s going to take some time for the public to learn more and see the real value.”

The momentum is also tied to a 2024 federal court ruling that stopped the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, a small financial regulator that monitors derivatives markets, from blocking bets on elections.

Geoffrey Skelley, chief elections analyst at Decision Desk HQ, called prediction market betting in the 2026 midterm elections “ the wild west right now .”

“We’re in real new territory, and it’ll be interesting to see how state and federal governments and others respond to it,” he added.

This underscores the worry among lawmakers about the possibility of corruption. Kalshi is reportedly investigating at least three trades placed on its platform shortly before news outlets began announcing Trump’s selection of his next press secretary, The Wall Street Journal reported.

Kalshi did not respond immediately to The Hill’s request for comment.

The Reuters/Ipsos poll was conducted from Sept. 30 to Oct. 5 among 4,506 respondents. The margin of error is 2.3 percentage points.
